Every vice, often committed, is treated lightly, and through habit is judged less serious. Just as grace illumines the mind, so the frequency of sin blinds reason. It is written: “Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand, lest they be converted and I heal them,” says the Lord. For when the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises them. No sin is so great that it does not seem light and small through habit.

Fourth, disordered cloisterers, through the habit of evil...

The blinded do not come to the grace of true compunction. They approach confession superficially, from habit alone. They have not abandoned their depraved will. They do not truly take up a resolution of amendment. Such people, buried in the habit of sin, do not fear the censure of strict examination; they do not withdraw from blindness of mind through the remedy of contrition. As they now despise the long-suffering goodness of God, so in that terrible hour they undergo the sentence of eternal death. What can confession of the mouth avail where there is no true contrition of heart? Without contrition, confession is not saving; nor can contrition exist without a resolution of amendment. The sign of contrition is the will to sin no more.

Fifth, the disordered citizens of the lowest region, made despisers of almighty God through the habit of sinning, continually fall into graver dangers of soul, because they always approach the most holy sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood in an evil manner. They make a superficial confession from habit; they allow the great beasts of vices to run through their senses. And thereafter, being in league with hell, they do not fear God; they despise the paths of amendment of life; they think themselves well ordered; they do not care with how many vices they are inwardly filled. Sometimes, sensibly moved by a fanciful devotion, they suppose that the Holy Spirit is now present; they affirm that they are beloved by God and holy. They impudently thrust themselves into the divine mysteries; not discerning the Lord’s body and blood, they receive them to judgment and condemnation.

Such people, communicating unworthily, are gravely hardened; they think themselves very secure and living well, and they do not duly care to cleanse their conscience from vices. Thus Judas the apostate did not fear boldly and shamelessly to complete the evil of betrayal which at first, as someone says, he feared to carry out against the Savior, after the morsel entered and the devil entered into him. O how many citizens of this lowest region there are: carnal monks, puffed up, proud, envious, murmurers, and entangled in various sins, whose conscience is rarely or never made clean by true contrition, and who nevertheless do not fear to approach the most holy altars almost every day.

Behold the evil company of all who dwell in this lowest region, whose end is destruction, for whom, after bodily death, a descent into hell is prepared. This is the far country of beastliness and unlikeness, into which that prodigal son went away, and squandered the portion of his inheritance luxuriously with harlots. In this region carnal citizens dwell, of whom the holy Apostle says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of God.” In this dark region, covered with the gloom of the dead, no spiritual good dwells; in it there is not peace, but beastly discord reigns, the prophet saying: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.”

Concerning Those Who, Being Near This Lowest Region, Often Fall Back [unclear] Through Inconstancy of Mind Although between the first region, which is evil, and the second, which is good, there is properly no middle, nevertheless there are some who often move between the two: at one time, from weakness, they are lukewarm; at another, from contrition of mind, they seem to be devout. These are weak people. Though they are not submerged in the lowest region, nevertheless through negligence they are very near it, and frequently indeed they fall into that evil habit, because they do not withdraw, as far as they can, from the affections of the flesh. Of these Bernard says in a certain sermon: “Pernicious lukewarmness, how dangerous it is, how troublesome and full of misery and grief, and plainly nearest to hell! It is rightly judged the shadow of death. Indeed, one finds people faint-hearted and slack, failing beneath the burden, needing rod and spurs; their joy is slack, their sadness faint-hearted, their compunction brief and rare; their thought is animal, their conduct lukewarm, their obedience without devotion, their speech without circumspection, their prayer without intention of heart, their reading without edification. Finally, as we see, fear of Gehenna scarcely restrains them, shame scarcely holds them back, reason scarcely bridles them, discipline scarcely keeps them in check. But if such people remain long under the burden, either they are crushed and succumb, or in a certain way they are in hell, so that they never fully breathe again into the light of the Lord’s mercies, nor into the freedom of the Spirit, which alone makes the yoke sweet and the burden light.” From there, however, [text breaks off] Vicious lukewarmness flows from the fact that the will has not yet been purified; they do not will the good as they know it, being drawn away and enticed by evil desire. For they love earthly little consolations in their flesh, whether in word, or in signs, or in deeds, or in something else; and even if this sometimes interrupts these things, it does not entirely break them off. Hence it is that they rarely direct their affections toward God, and their compunction is not continuous, but only for an hour.

But a soul that lies under these distractions cannot be filled with divine visitations; and the more it is emptied of the former, the more fully it will be filled with the latter. If much, much; if little, little. Or perhaps, if you prefer it put more strongly: these things will never be able to be mixed with those for eternity. For spirit and flesh do not dwell together, nor fire and lukewarmness in one dwelling, especially since lukewarmness itself is accustomed to provoke vomiting in the Lord.

Therefore whoever desires to flee from the midst of Babylon, whoever longs to come to the region of the spirit, should always take care to repel from himself the sluggishness of mind, and in holy purpose to burn continually with the fire of divine love. Nothing harms those who wish to serve God so much as lukewarmness of mind. It always arises at first from some small negligence, but unless it is cured at once, it grows wonderfully by degrees.

One who is placed near the lowest region always slips down into it, because the dregs of his former carnal way of life still subtly occupy his will, and on an easy occasion disturb his weak fervor of devotion. But no one can rise from the depth of hell with a lukewarm will; no one can overcome habit without a contrary habit, because unless some violence intervenes, the habit of sinning will always strengthen vice.

Rightly, then, this lowest region is called hell, since by a certain likeness of disturbance and aversion it is compared to hell. Now after this life there are three dwelling places of souls, which receive their citizens departing from the three regions and from this world.

The first dwelling place is called hell, and this is compared to the lowest region. For just as in hell no order, but perpetual horror, dwells, so in this lowest region all things are disturbed by the fury of a mind blinded by carnal affections. In hell all are evil, and in the lowest region nowhere are the good found. All who fall into hell have belonged to the lowest region. The lowest region always sends its citizens to the lower world, unless, led by penitence, while still living they have taken care to renounce dead works.

The second dwelling place is called purgatory, and this is compared to the second, rational region. For just as purgatory cleanses and perfects souls, and sends them, once purified, to the kingdom of heaven, so this second region washes its citizens, persevering within it through continual exercise, from the stains of sins, and disposes them for ascent to the third region, which is called spirit. In this dwelling place all are good, but still they must be purified so that they may become better; and in the second region nowhere are there evil people, but still they must always be exercised so that they may become better. This region sends its citizens who die within it to purgatory, because, even though all are good, they do not yet seem fit for the kingdom without temporal purification. For those who inhabit this middle region, however near they may seem to be to the highest, are still not yet entirely removed from the dust of the lower one.

The third dwelling place of the separated soul is called the kingdom of heaven, and this is compared to the highest region of the spirit. For just as in that heavenly homeland there is supreme rest and eternal peace, so in the region of the spirit there is continual tranquility of mind.

Here ends the first region.

Preface to the second tract of the first part, concerning the middle region, namely the rational region of cloistered persons.

But now let us at last leave the dark region of the carnal, in which the whirlwind of wickedness abides and the continual storm of vices. We have granted enough to it, and have lingered over it longer than our purpose had set. Let us therefore leave the dead to bury their dead; let us yield to the darkness; let us seek the light of the spiritual life. We must go out from the Egypt of the dark region; we must hasten diligently, through the middle way of reason, to the highest summit of the spirit. Let us therefore now at last approach the middle region of the soul, through which one comes gradually to the highest. This region of the soul is quite fittingly called rational, for in it there is continual labor in seeking the highest truth. The fervor of the mind in this middle region always strives to raise itself to higher things; but the weakness of the flesh, through the motion of the storm that follows, runs together with it to draw it back to lower things. From this comes continual labor; from this arise sighs and groans, because the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks on many things. This is the narrow way that leads to life, and few walk by it. In this region force is applied against the desires of the flesh until the will is subjected to the spirit at its nod. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” In this region the war of contest is declared for those who are to serve God; so the wise man bears witness: “Son,” he says, “when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation.” How great the temptations are in this middle region we learn daily through the difficulty of spiritual exercise, while, driven in various ways, we cannot remain long in fervor of spirit. Now the weakness of the flesh calls us back from the pursuit of progress; now the temptation of the ancient enemy troubles us; now the company of our neighbor hinders us; now the deceitfulness of the world seduces us. Therefore those who wish to make progress in this region of labor need the greatest fortitude, because no one can withstand his temptations to the end unless he studies daily to do violence to himself. But whoever thinks that he has come to this region must not presume on his own strength; for although the grace of God, in order to work good in us, requires the free choice of our will, so too the will necessarily requires grace. For no one is holy by his own strength. Therefore let no one dare to presume on himself, but let him who stands see that he does not fall. The life of the good upon the earth is warfare, for through many tribulations they come to the kingdom, and by the arduous labors of the virtues heaven is acquired. “Going,” says the prophet, “they went and wept, casting their seeds; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.” For whoever sows in tears shall reap in joy. But if anyone has failed in sowing, certainly he will not rejoice in the harvest. Since, therefore, through the continual labors of spiritual exercises the mind must be cleansed from the dust of the first region, let us not seek leisure in this middle region; let us not love the rest of negligence, because no one here is able to stand unless he girds himself strongly for continual labor. Whoever in this middle region does not always press on to better things soon falls back through negligence into the former habits of life; there he incurs the danger of failing where he has lost the appetite for making progress. This is the place of continual conflict; whoever neglects to fight in it retreats in order to be conquered.

The preface ends.

The second region of the soul begins, which is called rational, in which human beings are occupied amid many labors.

The second region of the soul, then, is called rational; in it the mind is exercised with continual labor in the search for the highest truth, and the farther it separates itself from the lowest region, the nearer it approaches the highest. And this region is set forth as resembling in certain ways the ethereal heaven, in which there is the position of the stars and continual motion.

For just as motion itself is always disposed in heaven by the order of the first mover as cause, so continual labor is exercised in the middle region, so that each intellectual power may be perfected in its own object and in no way depart from the order naturally implanted in it. There are three powers of this sort: memory, intellect, and will.

Of these, memory gathers the likenesses of things and their images, and extends itself toward what is arduous. The intellect, by discerning these images themselves, considers them, and here investigates the true. The will embraces what has been approved and ordered by the intellect, and it is occupied with the known good. When these three powers of the soul rightly keep their order, they lead the spirit by faith toward heavenly things.

The second region of life is compared to the ethereal heaven: for as in that heaven there is continual motion and the fixed position of the stars, so in this middle region there is motion and continual labor against the contests of vices. And as the motion of the stars fulfills the office appointed to it by nature in due order, so also in this region the equity of uprightness is required, so that each power of the soul, while subjected to its own object, may be perfected toward the end appointed for it, so far as this can happen to wayfarers.

But no power itself can be brought simply to fullness in this region, since no one in this pilgrimage is so perfect that he cannot become more perfect in his own order. For even if memory, in its own object, which is the arduous, could behold the gathered likenesses and images of all creatures, it would not be satisfied unless it could apprehend their principle, which is God. But this is altogether impossible in this region, in which we can form no images or likenesses of God. The intellect also, the counselor, so to speak, of the blind will, is extended toward the true; but however much it considers its own object, it is not satisfied until it can apprehend all truth and arrive, without the opinion of imaginative speculation, at knowledge of the eternal, highest, and unfailing truth. But that perfection is possible to none of the wayfarers so long as he remains in the body of mortality. The will too, although it is directed to its own object, which is the good, will not be able to be satisfied and truly gladdened unless it comes to that unchangeable and highest good, which no instability of change overshadows.

The highest truth and unchangeable good is God, who says to Moses: “Man shall not see me and live.” And the disciple of the highest truth says: “No one has ever seen God.” And the prophet, addressing the Lord, says: “Truly you are a hidden God.” But although the aforesaid three powers of the soul cannot perfectly comprehend their objects in this life, none of them ought to cease from its office, lest it incur the danger of failing in the very place where the task of striving has been appointed.

Therefore the citizens of this middle region mortify evil affections in themselves, adorn themselves with continual virtues, direct all their works by right intention, and in no way withdraw from the office of reason.

The citizens of this region are scholastic, contemplative, and active men, [unclear], devoted to honorable arts: they subject the sensual or carnal powers to reason; they keep these three powers of the soul clean from all unlawful objects; they always raise their intention toward the end of honorable goodness; and they reform the will, in act or in habit, toward its due end. Therefore the cenobite who loves this cleansing and desires to ascend to the third region of the spirit ought to consider and keep the following principal articles in the middle region.

The summary of the truth of this middle region is expressed in seven principal articles. Whoever desires to make progress in this middle region according to the vow of his profession should diligently take care to observe the following articles. If he neglects to keep them, he shows that he has not yet become a citizen of the middle region. For, as we said above, no one can remain in this middle region without a continual effort to advance; here not to make progress is to fall away, and not to have ascended is to descend. Therefore the monk who, having overcome the dark region, has at last, with God’s help, been able to reach this middle one...

he should beware lest he abandon the effort of advancing even a little, but always stretch toward further things; and he should remember the warning of the wise man, who says: “If you do not hold yourself steadfastly in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown,” that is, your conscience. For it is impossible for anyone to advance in holy conduct if he daily neglects to renew the effort of advancing through fear of the Lord. The ordered effect of this renewal is shown when the truth of the articles of the middle region is duly observed.

The first article, then, is the diligent intention of the cenobitic end; the second is the due restraint of the sensual powers; the third is the faithful cleansing of the powers; the fourth is the attentive reformation of the work of the lower region; the fifth is the ordered instruction in the progress of the true cenobite; the sixth is the adaptation of the powers for entry into the third region; and the seventh is the exemplary or experimental certainty of the aforesaid and of all things.

On the continual and diligent pursuit of the cenobitic end.

The first article.

Since the end is first in the intention of the wise man, and everything in its own kind is judged the more perfect the more closely it approaches its end, the monk who cultivates this middle region should always consider why he entered religion. If he finds his intention ordered, he should strive to continue it; but if he finds it corrupt, he should not fail to reform it according to the rectitude of the due end.

But note that in spiritual exercises the end is described as twofold, by which the virtue of monastic life is increased in merits. The first is charity, which is called the principal and ultimate end, to which all monastic exercises are ordered as to their first cause. Whatever good we do must always and principally be ordered to this end, because no work of virtue perfects merit unless charity always establishes the due foundation.

“God,” says John, “is charity; and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him.” And everyone who abides in God does not sin. The second end is dispositive toward the first and principal end, and is directed to it as a kind of intermediate fittingness; this is called secondary, or less principal. The monk must always attend to this too, and order his exercises through it to the ultimate end. For no one can lightly reach the end of principal charity if he neglects to observe the intermediate end.

This dispositive end toward the ultimate, so far as it pertains to cenobites, according to John Cassian in the Conferences of the Fathers, is to cast away from oneself entirely all the cares of the world, to mortify one’s own wills, to entrust every disposition of oneself to a prudent superior, and to take no thought for tomorrow. For in this middle region the cenobite must utterly reject his own will by taking up the denial of himself, and then resign himself totally into the hands of his prudent superior, so that within himself he may be clean from every impulse of his own will, and outwardly free from every secular occupation for serving the Lord. Indeed, unless the cenobite has come to this end, he is by no means a true monk, because he still sows corruption in corruptible flesh and in no way observes the virtue of his profession.

Next, the monastic denial of one’s own will seems principally to consist in three things, without which no one can truly be said to have denied himself. First, the mortification of the will requires in the monk the prior uprooting of his own judgment, because whoever relies on his own judgment or counsel disdains being humbly subject to another. For the root from which the defense of one’s own will first arises is called adherence to one’s own counsel or judgment. But whoever, while established in a monastery, desires to cling to his own judgment sins gravely in the Rule by usurping his own will. For it is fitting that the cenobite live by the command of others rather than by his own, if he desires to attain eternal life by the merit of obedience. Indeed, love of one’s own judgment is the greatest leprosy of the soul; according to Bernard, it is the more dangerous the more hidden it is, and the more [unclear].

the more someone has in abundance, the holier he seems to himself.

Second, mortification of the will requires the emptying out of one’s own affections, because no one can stand ordered amid adversities and comforts, and truly subject to God, who does not firmly restrain his carnal affections.

Third, for the mortification of one’s own will that poverty is required as hope, lest the monk’s affection be held captive by visible things, by food, clothing, and the rest; for whoever loves these things too much shows himself first to be a lover of pleasure against the rule. For the true cenobite of this [unclear], whose task is to devote himself fervently to the teaching of holy humility, must gladly despise all worldly things for the love of God, and love absolutely nothing except for God. If he has anything for use, with the rule allowing it, let him beware of setting the affection of his heart upon it; let him be ready, at the judgment of his shepherd and for the usefulness of the brothers, to surrender everything with a peaceful heart. Let him always choose the things that are simple and lowly, give thanks to God in all things, and, placing his hope and sufficiency in him alone, say cheerfully: “In you, Lord Jesus, I have all things; for love of you I gladly despise all things; I shall care nothing at all for passing things.”

Therefore let our devout cenobite always direct the faithful eye of his consideration toward this end of his monastic institution and intention; let him never withdraw from the sight of it, because whoever forgets the final end in his action wanders like an unskilled and blind sailor amid the storms of the sea, soon to perish. Let the faithful monk, then, imitate the sailor experienced in devotion, so that just as the sailor, always having the harbor before his eyes, strives with intent solicitude to steer his ship there, so the mind of a good man may always be directed to God, as to its shore and final end.

Archers set up for themselves some fixed mark, and lest their sight be scattered away from the target, they close one eye. And just as the arrow of the shooter is aimed at the mark, so the intention of the good monk is always ordered toward God; in that intention the eye of lower affection must also be closed, lest the sharpness of higher contemplation be scattered through empty things. For we must close ourselves, as though in unknowing, to the affection for earthly curiosities and to the understanding of carnal wisdom, if we desire always to be lifted up by the gaze of the mind toward our proper end.

And just as the eagle is said to gaze upon the sun with eyes that are not dazzled, so the monk, the servant of God, contemplates without interruption the end of the monastic institution. As the prudent wayfarer, while proceeding with delight, considers the dwelling toward which he is going, so the good cenobite, in everything he does, always pants with fervent desire chiefly toward his own end, which is God. But foolish is the traveler who, though placed on the road, forgets the dwelling toward which he is going and, wandering, knowingly entangles himself in the various hindrances of others. And the monk who does not diligently consider the end of his destination is certainly blind and wanders off on the road.

Therefore the good monk and lover of his own salvation does not neglect his good effort in spiritual exercises, but, always striving in affection toward higher things, raises himself up by exercising himself in holy works. Good effort is this: to omit nothing of what God has commanded; to obey the shepherd humbly in all things for the love of God; to lift up the affection, always drawn away from earthly things, to the memory of heavenly things; and through the continual exercise of spiritual conduct to renew his holy resolve daily. Whatever good the devout cenobite does, let him always offer it with faithful attention to almighty God; let him despise all earthly things with a strong spirit; let him long to please God alone.

Let the faithful intention of the cenobitic life always be that he desire and long for nothing other than the praise and honor of God; let his attention be so diligent that he knows how to summon all the senses of the body and the affections of the soul to the service of God, so that he may faithfully serve his God and seek his glory, not his own.

On the due restraint of the sensual powers. Article 2.

For it is useful and also necessary for us to restrain the powers of sensual passions; among monks I think almost no one is ignorant of this. Indeed, whoever desires to reach the due end of regular life which we have described in this region must subdue, with prudent constancy, his disordered natural habits and movements, because no one can truly resign himself to another’s command if he does not firmly restrain the powers of sensual passions. One who desires to make progress must leave behind, with steadfast mind, both the movements and the prudence of the flesh, and show himself a son of divine grace, not of flesh and blood. For Scripture says: If you live according to the command of the flesh, you will die. Indeed, those who sow in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. But flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. But what does the Savior say to us? “A man’s enemies,” he says, “are those of his own household.” And who are these members of his household except the sensual powers that oppose the spirit? For concupiscibility and irascibility, our enemies, stir up within us all evils against the spirit and continually disturb the house of conscience with various passions. For as long as these sensual powers carry out their natural movements and courses in a man, they do not allow him to ascend to the freedom of the spirit. Concupiscibility enjoys the delights in the sense of the flesh, and, on the contrary, the irascible power detests the bodily hardships. Meanwhile, as long as this war of the flesh is waged in a man, he is regarded as a restless, carnal monk and a dweller in the lowest region. Therefore whoever desires to come to eternal life must firmly restrain these disordered powers of sense in all things.

Therefore the faithful cenobite strives to direct the concupiscible power toward hardships that are acceptable to God, and to reform all his affections according to God’s good pleasure. If he does this, he will pray confidently to the Lord: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times.” And, sweetly weeping, he will cry out that other saying: “As the deer longs for the fountains of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” Then let him learn prudently to attach the irascible power to God, to set it against sensual delights, and to reform it diligently toward hatred of vices. Thus the soul, ordered toward its principle, will not fear to endure any hardships for the love of God, and by means of the irascible power it will begin to resist firmly all carnal desires. And then the devout cenobite, with his spirit lifting itself up, will cry: “My soul refused to be comforted.” And that saying of the Apostle: “I have counted all things as dung.” For the soul that truly loves God despises everything except him.

From these two powers every disordered affection arises; and good affections likewise are generated from them in the contrary way. For joy and hope take their beginning from the concupiscible power, and the irascible power brings forth sorrow and fear. Saint Bernard speaks of these thus: “The whole heart of man is governed by four affections; if we bring these back to God, the whole heart of man is converted.”

On the Faithful Cleansing of the Powers Article Three Since we are by no means able to restrain the sensual powers unless we also faithfully cleanse the intellectual powers, great and continual diligence is needed for this cleansing, because the cenobite who is weakened by the torpor of negligence is never cleansed from vicious affections. For one who sows with corrupted powers brings back nothing else from his errors but corruption. Therefore the cenobite, the inhabitant of this middle region, must correct his higher powers from every disorder, if he wishes to remain constantly in the pursuit of progress. These intellectual powers must be cleansed in this way.

First, the intellect must be purged of every imagining of empty likenesses, so that it may [unclear] from union.

freeing it from material things, raise it upward, without any image of likeness, to its own principle; and, prudently intent upon its object, turn its whole self toward the highest rule of truth.

Then let our faithful cenobite not neglect to strip his memory of every occupation with an unlawful thing. Let him admit no forms of thought that are shameful or less useful; let him strive to repel the phantasms of irrational passions and [unclear] meditations, and, so far as can be done, to think nothing foolish.

The will also must be purified from every disordered affection, so that it wills nothing except what right reason suggests should be willed, and rejects nothing except what reason, according to the judgment of truth, forbids it.

But this restraint of virtue and cleansing of the powers, without which we say that no one can advance at all, is granted only through diligence great, discerning, and constant in a strong battle. We know that the kingdom of God suffers violence, and no one can subject the enemy to himself unless he has resolved to fight against him fiercely and perseveringly. For we have learned from the testimony of the blessed pontiff Augustine that a man does not die well unless he has first died to vices and desires. But no one truly dies to these among men unless he resists his own wills through continual labor, sowing in tears. Therefore the soul must be fortified with saving doctrines; the strength of patience must be taken up in all things. For just as a naked man, unarmed and impatient of labor, cannot overthrow an armed enemy, so a monk without spiritual arms and without a certain continual force of fighting cannot cleanse his intellectual powers in any childish way. Now although the arms of spiritual warfare are many in its progress, three especially must be taken up by the monk.

First, indeed, vigor is necessary for the cenobite in all that he does, so that he may bravely dare things contrary to the flesh, and in no way grow lukewarm in his holy purpose. For spiritual exercises are hard and altogether contrary to the flesh, and he who scorns to put on most strongly the arms of vigor is not enough to persevere constantly in them. Therefore, if you desire to subject all your affections to the spirit, if you wish to fight successfully against the vices of the flesh, take care to do prudent violence to yourself and to arm yourself bravely against all things.

Next, a certain holy severity must be taken up by you, through which all contrary and adverse things of this world are borne as though they were nothing. For truly, whoever for love of God and desire for heavenly things has once genuinely taken up this kind disposition of the soul, no longer fears any adversities of the flesh; rather, he is so deeply filled within by contemplation of the divine reward that he seems to delight more in adversities that occur than in prosperity.

But severity is by no means pleasing to the weak unless it has been somewhat tempered by the sweetness of kindness. Therefore kindness itself must next be taken up by the soldier, so that when, tempted in battle by the weakness of the flesh, or even wounded, he sometimes wavers, he may soon rise again through repentance to fight once more with greater strength. For the soldier of Christ, if he falls in battle, must rise again through contrition and the other remedies of penance as often as necessary, to fight again, until at last, at some time, by God’s mercy, he is able to overcome the adversary. If the just man falls seven times in a day and rises again, how should the sinner, now penitent, not hope for pardon? Rise, soldiers, to fight again as often as you have fallen when the adversary has conquered. Always renew the warfare more strongly from the beginning, so that the enemy whom you cannot yet destroy by strength, you may at last overcome by perseverance. Do not despair of victory, faithful cenobite, because you have often been conquered by temptation and vice and have fallen into the snare. Do not lie prostrate any longer because you feel yourself weak, but rise again as often as you have fallen, and trust that you have a merciful Lord, by whose help you will at last be victorious against the adversary. For no one suddenly becomes perfect, nor does God grant immediate victory over the enemy to incautious soldiers, lest those who are about to perish fall into grave pride.

A possession acquired with difficulty is always held dearer, and a good that is acquired laboriously is guarded with greater diligence. Thus the loving Father, God, permits us, when conquered by the temptations of the adversary, to fall for a time into the pit of sin through alternating reversals, until, conscious of our weakness, we learn to hope in nothing in our own strength, but only in his grace. But you, man, who often interrupt your progress by sinning, never delay to rise again; for even if you cannot perfectly subject the enemy to yourself, it will nevertheless be good for you if the last day can find you standing and fighting, even after a frequently repeated fall. But this counsel does not release those to whom the mercy of God has granted strength and grace for defeating the adversary. Nevertheless, let him who stands take heed lest he fall.

On the attentive reform of the works of the first region.

Article Two.

Since, as we taught at the end of the first treatise, this middle region is nearest to the lowest part of the first region, in which, if the cenobite has been even a little negligent and remiss, he immediately falls back again without interval into the former region. And therefore whoever desires to persevere in this region by making progress should always strive, with attentive vigilance, to reform the works of the lower region. And, lest we be lengthy, whoever desires to exercise this reform in himself should take up, in this region, works contrary to the eight articles of the first region. For, as is taught by the tradition of physicians, contraries are cured by contraries.

Therefore faithful monks, citizens of this middle region, are first commanded to look to this: that each strive before all things to order himself toward God. This ordering is said to be done well when God, according to the law, is loved with the whole heart above all things.

Next, the devout cenobite should keep himself ordered toward his prelate, offer him humility and reverence, strive to love him with sincere charity, and observe according to the Rule all that he commands.

The rector also, [unclear] of souls, should take care to walk in ordered fashion toward the cenobites, to show himself a shepherd to the sheep and not a hireling, not to neglect the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, and not to set temporal things before spiritual things. Let him hate vices, love the brothers, and show himself an example to all in every good thing.

Next, let brothers cling to one another as members of one head; let them love one another mutually in the true charity of God, and not withdraw from good zeal. For all of us who trust, through the faith of Christ, to come to eternal life by persevering in good works are members of Christ, the supreme head. But whoever pursues his brother with evil zeal or hatred and other evil affections first separates himself from the head, and then does injury to Christ.

Consequently, let each one show himself ordered toward himself: let him humbly subject himself to all for the love of Christ, prefer others to himself through humility, and believe himself more unworthy than all monks.

In the use of the things of the monastery, let them always take care not to exceed the institution of the Rule, but strive everywhere to show themselves ordered and faithful in all things. Let no one have or seek anything contrary to the will of the abbot; let him admit no pleasure into his soul in the use of things.

Then faithful cenobites should take care to order themselves, according to the institution of the Rule, to contempt of the world, so that they love nothing in this world, but truly despise all things for the love of God.

Let them never neglect to order themselves most diligently to penance; let them often have recourse to humble confession of their faults. For just as no one is believed to live in this world without sin, so penance is judged necessary for all, even monks. Therefore the good cenobite, through the practice of compunction, will always have recourse to penance, humbly accuse himself of his faults in chapter, willingly perform the penance imposed, and faithfully amend himself in all things.

On the rightly ordered formation of the true monastic spirit and the degrees of humility. Article V.

The monk’s first virtue is humility, and pride is the gravest crime in a cenobite. For a monk who is proud with a swollen mind becomes an imitator and servant of the devil, and is stripped of all virtues, if he had any, because no virtue can remain in a mind in which pride happens to dwell. Therefore the cenobite who desires to make progress in this middle region should learn to order himself through humility toward the true progress of monastic formation, because no one truly attains humility except one who devotes himself to spiritual exercises.

True progress in regular formation, excluding all adulterous Muses, arises from the degrees of humility, which are set down through their roots as twelve in the Rule. The roots of this progress come from the practice of sacred reading, which gradually leads a man to the fear of the Lord. From reading arises spiritual meditation; from it holy compunction is generated. The more useful mode of cenobitic meditation consists in the memory of the Lord’s passion and in the consideration of the benefits of God. But those who pass beyond this middle region and come to tranquility of spirit make their meditations more sublime through contemplation of the divine majesty and excellence. We shall speak of these in their proper place.

These two roots receive increase from the watering of continual prayer and grow strong into the firmness of a most sturdy plant. For no meditation makes progress without prayer, and study without it will never save.

From these three roots of spiritual progress arises the fear of the Lord, which is the first degree of humility; from it the other degrees are begotten, succeeding in order. But monks who neglect the saving study of the Scriptures and holy meditations with continual prayers by no means arrive at this first degree of humility. And he who cannot climb the first degree of humility, how will he be able to come to the others? For the second is never climbed if the first is neglected. Therefore he who neglects one climbs none.

The study of sacred reading must not be undertaken for the vanity of the world, nor for the pleasure of a seduced mind, because reading never advances toward compunction when the delight of the flesh or of vanity has corrupted it. A monk, through the study of sacred reading, cannot reach devotion unless he strives to change all curiosity into a simple spirit. Therefore whoever desires to advance from the reading of Scripture to compunction, whoever wishes to ascend to humility through the roots of fear, must not choose just any material for reading, but only that which can more greatly stir the mind to the love of God.

For this purpose the reading of the lives of the saints seems to me sufficiently suitable, because the mind of one lying low is often raised to the love of God when the life of his servants is recalled to memory. We gladly admit their miracles and revelations concerning the torments or joys of separated souls, when they conform to the Catholic faith, because we have learned by experience that sluggish hearts are often stirred by them to compunction. Finally, the passions of the holy martyrs arouse the fervor of devotion in no small measure; in them, when we bring to mind the unconquerable charity of Christ, pierced by the example of such constancy and touched as if by a certain fire of love, we sigh over our imperfection.

From reading the material of meditation is taken; and as the former has been, so the latter will be. The shameful songs of poets, the curious doctrines of philosophers, and the swollen writings of rhetoricians do not arouse the fervor of devout compunction in monks, but rather suffocate what has been conceived. Therefore, if you wish to devote yourself to good meditation, do not occupy your mind with readings other than holy and devout ones. Indeed, grapes are not gathered from thorns, nor is compunction generated from the pursuit of vanity. Let him who studies for the knowledge of this world read the things that suit his learning; but let him who seeks compunction [unclear].

Let him read the things that kindle the soul to the love of God through fear. Therefore let frequent reading on the last things that await us take its beginning from fear; then let the deeds of the holy fathers be read, so that the memory of the future may strike the mind with fear of God, and the conduct of holy examples may kindle the desire to imitate them. For the wise man says: “Remember your last things, and you will not sin.” The conduct of the holy fathers is set before us as an example, and the destruction of the wicked is recounted for our instruction, so that rewarded virtue may stir desire, and punished iniquity may forbid license to sin.

Therefore let the devout cenobite call to mind the examples and virtues of the saints; let him consider the brief pleasure of the wicked, but their eternal torment, so that by fearing unhappiness he may deserve to escape it, and by persisting in virtues obtain that everlasting joy. The distinct condition of the good and the wicked is no slight matter, since it is described as truly enduring forever and is ended by no limit. O eternity, always to be feared by mortals: in it, after this life has been completed, there is no fear for the just, and no hope of deliverance for the wicked. Let him who can consider what eternity is, where there is no end; let him who dares imagine a limit; and when in eternity he finds nothing other than eternal, let him understand that all the time in which he lives in this world is nothing. For indeed, once the spirit has been driven from the flesh, it is necessarily compelled to enter this abyss of eternity; and the condition which it has once received according to its merits it will bear without end and will not be changed into another. For he who dies good in the charity of God will obtain eternal life according to his merits. But he who, evil and without the reconciliation of repentance, has once departed from this life, will remain with the demons in hell, to be tormented without end.

From these meditations servile fear arises in the mind, through which one gradually comes to love. But so that we may successively lead cenobites through these roots to charity, it pleases us to explain briefly, in order, the degrees of humility described in the Rule.

The first degree of humility described by Saint Benedict in the Rule is the fear of God, which is called the beginning of wisdom. Fear, however, is handed down with a threefold distinction: namely, servile, initial, and filial, which is also called chaste. From this threefold distinction three roots are spoken of, according to which the beginning cenobite ought to order his meditations. For each root has its own proper meditations, and when one is rightly disposed, another better one is always generated.

From servile fear, if it is taken up not merely servilely but prudently and virtuously, come meditations on terrors and punishments, which, by restraining the soul from sin, gradually introduce it to love. For when the mind is turned to horror by the consideration of punishments, boldness in sinning is restrained, because the servant who fears blows keeps the commands of his lord. This servile fear, however, is not sufficient for meriting the paternal inheritance; yet as an initial effect it is disposed toward filial fear, which is sufficient.

Initial fear is placed midway between the two, and from the third it is easily changed into filial fear. This initial fear receives meditations on the last things, and both fears to incur punishments and trembles to lose the sweet fatherland. And this place is set down in the Rule, where its roots are also described.

Filial fear, however, gathers its meditations into love, since it fears nothing except that the beloved father be offended. Of this fear the wise man says: “The fear of the Lord is glory and boasting, gladness and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and will give gladness and joy and length of days.” And again: “It will be well with him who fears God at the last, and on the day of his death he will be blessed.” This fear is called chaste because it detests evil not from fear of punishments, but from love alone.

From this threefold fear we see three exercises and spiritual breadths arise concerning the degrees of humility, and individual exercises correspond to the individual fears. For one Servile fear performs its exercises; initial fear applies itself to virtues; and filial fear proceeds much differently in its works. For just as affections come to the heart in various ways, so the exercises of one fear take place in different ways. For the publican feared the judge’s sentence in one way, through the memory of himself and of his sins; Jerome said that in another way he seemed to hear the sound of the trumpet calling the dead to judgment. And concerning the former the holy Gospel says: Standing far off, the publican would not lift up his eyes to heaven, but, striking his breast, said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” But that blessed Jerome said: “Whether I drink or eat, I always think that I hear that trumpet sounding in my ears: ‘Rise, you dead; come to judgment.’” The compunction of both arises from fear, but both are not begotten from the desire of one and the same affection. For the publican, terrified by the guilt of sins and by the sentence of the just judge, feared, and therefore, pierced with compunction, said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” Jerome, however, is not shaken by fear from consciousness of guilt, but, founded in charity and reckoning himself an unprofitable servant, reveres the abyss of divine justice.

The second degree is to abandon one’s own will for love of God, and not to love one’s own willing in anything against the rule. This degree arises from the first ascent of humility and lifts one up to the third. For truly, he who fears God, and truly dreads being separated from him and undergoing punishments, hates nothing more than his own will. For the faithful cenobite knows that every sin arises from self-will alone, and therefore he detests it as the gate of hell. For that blessed man truly said: Take away self-will, and there will be no hell. For nothing burns in hell except self-will; nothing loses the grace of God except voluntary fault. Therefore whoever truly fears God and dreads losing his grace begins to fear his own will as the ambusher of the soul. The consideration of the danger of self-will makes the cenobite despise his own willing and deny himself. And this denial of self-will and of oneself is perfected in three ways, as will be said in what follows.

First, he denies himself to himself who strives to live according to the teaching of eternal wisdom and not according to his own impulses, and to obey Christ, who persuades him to humility in all things. Therefore let the Savior say to the cenobite: If you wish truly to deny yourself to yourself and follow me, take away your eyes, lest they see harmful things; your ears, lest they hear vain things; and in place of the sweet things of this world, take bitter things. Learn to despise the pleasures of your body; to love tranquility and peace of heart; to receive all tribulations patiently and joyfully for love of me; and to desire to be seen by all as vile and contemptible. Learn accordingly to break your wills in all things, to mortify the desires of the flesh, to despise all earthly things, and, as far as can be done, to conform your life with all your strength to the way of life of your Savior. For he who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk just as he walked. Whoever has done these things has well denied himself.

Second, the denial of self-will is then rightly perfected when the advantages of others are set before one’s own. For the holy apostle says: “Not seeking the things that are your own, but the things that are others’.” For according to the saying of Bernard, the soul is laid down for the brethren as often as their advantages are preferred to one’s own benefits for love of God.

Third, the resignation of self-will receives the fullness of perfection when the cenobite, pierced with compunction and wholly handed over to God, desires out of love to serve him most gratefully without regard for reward. And this most holy resignation of self-will makes a man near to God and always rests in his love.

But just as this resignation of oneself receives its substance from the second degree of humility, so also it necessarily requires inward and complete resignation to the will of God in all things. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me.” Perfect resignation, therefore, is that by which the human will is totally subjected to the divine will and, out of whole love, [unclear].

Thus indeed the Lord himself taught us to pray: “Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” And that saying of the psalmist: “Into thy hands I commend my spirit.” Never is one safer in this world than when the human will is perfectly subjected to God.

Indeed, perfect surrender of oneself, by which the cenobite truly subjects his will to God, shows without intermediary the right way to the highest good. Here there is the greatest tranquillity of mind; the greatest security is present in the heart, because the soul that strives to subject itself perfectly to God will no longer be able to fear any opposition of this world, except sin alone. Whatever adversity comes upon him, with the Lord’s help he has learned to overcome; whatever comfort he desires, he understands that he possesses it in the Lord alone. He despises all adversities for love of him; he has placed all good things in love of him. For that devout man wisely said: “Leave all things, and you will find all things; abandon desire, and you will find true peace.”

Finally, so that this surrender of one’s own will may receive the fullness of consummation, it seeks, to pass over the rest, the aid of a threefold support.

The first is placed in the virtue of perseverance: that the will, once renounced, never be resumed. For that holy Bernard says to those who despise this support: “Why do you again take charge of yourselves, who once, after mature deliberation, handed over your will to us?” For the monk who has once handed his will over to God in the hands of the abbot does not resume it without the crime of sacrilege.

The second thing required for perfect surrender of the will is that it never be relaxed. Hence the Lord says to the lukewarm soul in the Apocalypse: “I have a few things against you, because you have left your first charity,” that is, your fervor.

Third, surrender of the will will be perfected if it is never revoked. For the Savior says: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Therefore, when you see a cenobite restless or stirred by anger, know that the whole mass of temptation proceeds from lack of resignation; nor will you ever cure this sickness unless you first persuade him to the surrender of his renounced will.

The third degree of humility is to submit oneself to a superior in all obedience for the love of God, and to show oneself an imitator of Christ by deeds, not only by words. Of him the holy Apostle says: “He was made obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” This degree takes its beginning from the second and raises its ascent to the third. For as the second mortifies one’s own will by renouncing it, so this one lays the foundation of holy work through humble subjection. The former subjects the whole self to the divine will; this one, for the love of God, obeys even men.

The keeping of one degree without observance of the other is not enough in a monk; nor is the will of a cenobite subjected to the divine ordinance if it disdains to obey the command of a superior. Therefore the true cenobite, placing all his joy in the virtue of holy obedience, thinks it the greatest gain to fulfill in all things the will of his pastor; he believes that he incurs grave damage to his soul if he finds that he has committed himself even a little outside obedience. With faithful devotion he always considers what the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” Hence that blessed Bernard says to monks: “Whatever a man commands in God’s place must be received no differently than if God himself commanded it in person.” Therefore let the true monk prefer this subjection of obedience to every sacrifice, let him do absolutely nothing against its integrity, and let him continually say within himself what is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices.” Hence the Rule also says: “Therefore all things are to be done with the abbot’s will.”

But this degree, as we have said, arises from the second, because he who has first perfectly renounced his own will out of fear of God now seeks nothing else in this world than to follow that will in all things. But because God speaks once and does not repeat the same thing, and weak man cannot know the will of the Most High, therefore he entrusts himself [unclear].

[unclear] into the hands of his prelate. Let the cenobite therefore obey according to the rule, and, obeying the vicar of Christ, he undoubtedly fulfills the will of God.

Obedience to prelates must be kept strictly according to the Gospel and the monastic rule; for although the mutual obedience of the brethren is good, surely it is not to be preferred to the command of a superior. Monks are ordered to render discreet obedience to one another, and, while preserving the commands of superiors, to anticipate one another in mutual service. To take an example from our own custom: obedience is owed to all according to order. If a brother calls on you, obey gladly; if another, a senior, commands you, leave aside the command of the first and obey him. Again, if the prior of the community intervenes with his command, all mutual obedience of the brethren will cease. But if the abbot’s command intervenes, no obedience to anyone else will have force against it. For he is believed to act first in Christ’s place in the monastery, and therefore he is preferred to all.

There are seven graded circumstances of the holy virtue of obedience, which blessed Bernard described. The first degree of obedience is to obey willingly, so that you have no will of your own at all, but believe your shepherd’s good pleasure to be wholly your own. The second is to obey simply, so that you do neither more nor otherwise than what has been commanded you, nor omit anything by doing less. The third is to obey cheerfully, so that you show serenity in your face and sweetness in your voice. The fourth is to obey swiftly, so that the hand is not slower in the work than the command is in the voice. The fifth is to obey manfully, lest one withdraw his strength from the command and pretend to be weak and unequal to the precepts. The sixth is to obey humbly: not proudly, not arrogantly, not contentiously; for unless obedience is humble, it will receive not reward but punishment. The seventh is to obey perseveringly, because that obedience is not true which is interrupted before completion; and only he who perseveres to the end is rewarded.

The fruit of obedience is everlasting and is never bounded by any end. Almighty God obeys our prayers only insofar as we obey our superiors. Do not flatter yourself, stiff-necked monk, because of persistence in prayer, for Christ does not hear the prayer of one who despises Christ’s vicar in the monastery. Humility raises prayer; obedience commends it. For obedience, as one of the fathers said, is the salvation of all the faithful, the mother of all virtues, the finder of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens, closes the gates of hell, becomes a fellow-dweller with the angels, and possesses the food of all the saints. But the monk who casts off subjection to obedience runs toward death.

The fourth degree of humility is patience in adversities. Our holy father Benedict speaks of this in the Rule: if a monk, under obedience, embraces patience with silent conscience in hard and contrary things, or even in any injuries inflicted on him. This degree also takes its beginning from the third, since no one is truly to be called obedient if he is found impatient. For as lord Chrysostom says, he cannot be acceptable to the king who has been subject to the enemy; nor is he truly subject to Christ who has been marked by the passion of impatience. For no one will be able to conquer a fierce enemy unless he has learned to fight bravely against him. Patience is very necessary for us, since no virtue perfects the one who reads if patience deserts him. It is also, as blessed Gregory teaches, a mark of greater merit to endure adversities patiently for God and to toil in good works. And Saint Jerome says: He who thinks that tribulation has come upon him for his sins calls forth God’s mercy more fully toward doing good. Therefore let the cenobite learn to oppose the virtue of patience to all accidents, if he desires to triumph over his enemies. He who suffers conquers; he who murmurs is overcome.

In three things, however, the virtue of patience is especially necessary, and the rewards are very high: in insults [unclear].

The patience of a prudent man who loves God preserves the purpose of humility: in the removal of goods and temporal advantages it receives increase, and in bodily injury the silent consciousness of virtue preserves its undertaking. Consider now, faithful soul, how your most loving Savior Jesus endured these three things most patiently for your redemption; and if you believe that you love him, do not think it burdensome, for love of him, to endure similar things with patience.

From the three grades immediately preceding we establish one sum of the cenobitic end, which, that it may seem reasonable to us, we call the threefold grade. For by three grades, namely the second, third, and fourth, the end of the cenobitic institution is fulfilled, and the earlier renunciation of pleasure is brought to completion. For where patience, the guardian of the virtues, is joined to the earlier renunciation of pleasure and to obedience, every pleasure and care of the body is mortified. Whoever has deserved to ascend this threefold grade has fulfilled the Lord’s command, by which he says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” through the second grade of humility; “and take up his cross,” through the third; “and follow me,” through the fourth.

The fifth grade of humility is true confession of sin. A faithful cenobite is said to ascend to this if he confesses to his abbot, with humble trust, all evil thoughts that come into his heart, or any evil deeds committed in secret. For if anyone, through impatience and at the adversary’s prompting, sins in the preceding threefold grade, in this one he is restored through contrition and humble confession. For no one is found so perfect that he never contracts the stain of earthly conduct, as Scripture says: “In many things we all offend.” For no one is clean from sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day. Therefore this grade necessarily follows immediately after the fourth, and in it all the negligences of the preceding grades are amended. True confession lifts up the soldier who falls in battle, heals the one wounded by the enemy, and strengthens the weak and faint-hearted. Therefore whoever desires to stand in battle and bravely conquer the enemy should more often have recourse to the defenses of true confession. For it is impossible for one wounded by the enemy to recover health if he neglects to reveal the wound itself to the physician. Therefore you, faithful cenobite, who desire to save your soul and to be a good soldier of Jesus Christ, do not omit humble confession, because you will never be able to conquer the devil better than if you are zealous to disclose faithfully to your abbot all the thoughts he suggests to you and your sins. It is certain to me, and proved by much experience, that a cenobite hands himself over to be greatly conquered by temptations when he refuses to keep this grade.

The sixth grade of humility arises from true confession: namely, that the monk judge himself vile and unworthy for all things. For according to the Rule we believe him to be a true monk whom we see content with every vileness and extremity in food, clothing, and humble patience. Vileness is referred to common useful things, but extremity is placed in abject and heavier hardships. For he gladly embraces with patience those things that are viler in clothing, food, and all necessities of the body; he delights in all things: to serve the sick, the foul, lepers, and the rejected; to be confounded, degraded, and despised. Therefore the monk who is truly dead to the flesh and the world should be content with every vileness and extremity, should show himself a faithful worker in all things, and should also believe himself vile and unworthy because of the corruption of nature, by which he offends in many things. For indeed, whatever good we do in this world, however holy and religiously we live in this age, it cannot suffice to merit eternal life unless the great mercy of God deigns to come to our aid. We receive the greatest things for the least: we expect the kingdom of God not as owed to us from our merit, but as promised from grace. For the holy Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.” But if we are judged without mercy by the justice of God, we are worthy of hell. We all incur wrath by sin, but we bring back love from grace. No one is saved except by grace; no one [unclear].

[Unclear] except through justice. Meanwhile, however, if we are to obtain the grace of God, he requires the efforts of our good will; without that grace nothing in us works toward merit. For although no one is holy by his own powers, nevertheless no one does good well unwillingly. Thus the grace of God and freedom of choice stand in relation to one another, and one without the other cannot suffice for saving a human being; both must necessarily come together for the working of virtue. Therefore, since without the grace of God we can do nothing good, we ought to consider ourselves worthless and unworthy of all things, so that, when we submit ourselves to God in humility, we may always obtain greater gifts. And therefore this sixth degree of confession is one of merit and the single foundation of all the preceding ones. For as long as the cenobite remains in this degree of humility, he will stand firm in the earlier ones.

The seventh degree of humility is not only to believe, from the inmost affection of the heart, that one is lower than all, but also to desire, with a simple mind, that others believe and say this about him. This condition of holy humility sets one on high, and in this time it is loved by few monks. The first condition of this deep humility seems to consist in this: that the monk ought from his heart to reckon himself lower than all. The second is that he should rejoice to be reckoned worthless and abject by all, and should desire this without pretense from the inmost affection of his heart. The third condition is placed in a higher dwelling: namely, that with the same affection the monk should delight to be treated most contemptibly and to be trampled on by all. Rooted in this humility, the cenobite loves reproach and insult; he does not fear being despised and most contemptibly abused, because, submitting himself wholly in the love of God, he humbly takes his place, and hastens to insults as though to banquets, with the greatest cheerfulness. But so that you may understand the truth of this seventh degree, read the following considerations.

The first consideration directs the mind toward hope in divine love, which arises from a certain pious confidence. Although a person may never know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless each person can in some way recognize, from the disposition of his own heart, what he ought to think about his own state, whether good or bad.

Second, one must consider that through a good disposition of heart and an orderly will toward God, love of God and approval by the good are signs.

Thus, when he was born in the flesh, the angels sang: Peace on earth to people of good will.

Third, it must be noted that just as a good disposition of heart always orders and summons the mind through holy exercises toward the fear of God and the practice of virtues, so the carelessness of an evil disposition inclines it especially toward vices and sloth. Reflection on this difference provides a conjecture.

Fourth, one must consider that an evil disposition of heart hinders and empties out the grace of God and merits in a person, because it makes the soul base, ignoble, and degenerate, and always disposes it toward graver and worst things. Indeed, the root of evils of tongue and deed comes from an evil heart, as is clear in Saul and many similar cases.

The fifth consideration is that evil of deed and tongue is never properly examined unless the evil of the heart is first truly known. Each person can examine his own heart better than another’s, and consider what kind of person lies hidden within himself. Therefore it is enough for the cenobite to whom care of another has not been entrusted to inspect his own heart diligently, and in no way to occupy himself with scrutiny of another’s heart. But the shepherd, or the monk to whom the care of souls is entrusted, must also know the face of his flock.

Sixth, from these things it must be noted that it is very rash to wish to examine another’s heart, and from words and deeds to judge the inner thoughts of the brothers. The Lord knows those who are his, and it is not granted to a human being, apart from the reason of his office, to become a rash judge of another’s heart.

Seventh, it must be noted that a small evil of one’s own heart, known in oneself, harms more than a great evil suspected doubtfully in another’s heart. For the former must be corrected, because it is certain and known; the latter must be piously excused, because it is unknown.

Eighth, one must consider that, since each person sees many imperfections in his own heart which he cannot see in others, recognize this: on account of these things, insofar as they are obstacles to grace, he ought to reckon himself lower than others. But insofar as they defile the soul, let him despise himself as more worthless, even if he knows their public crimes. For since the roots of the heart are utterly unknown to him, he cannot know how the divine election concerning that person was ordained from eternity. Who would have believed that the thief crucified with God was elect from eternity, if he judged him according to his works? All things turn out for the good of the elect, since where he sees sin to have abounded, often by the will of divine election greater grace is found. For divine love regards and embraces its elect from eternity, and looks upon them as elect not according to the misery in which they now are, but according to their future glory. Therefore, cenobite, beware of slandering others; beware of judging others, if you desire to escape eternal death. For who are you, that you judge another’s servant? He stands to be judged by his God alone.

Now the disposition of this seventh degree, because of that clause “from the innermost affection of the heart,” has a threefold root of its origin: namely, truth, hope, and charity. For when the faithful cenobite sees that he does not have his being from himself, he truly thinks himself, insofar as he is from himself, to be nothing; and consequently, in the same respect, he considers his works, insofar as they are from himself, who is nothing, to be nothing, since he knows that nothing comes from nothing. Therefore the monk who, in this respect, regards himself and his works as nothing does not dare to depart from the truth, because he fears falling into the vice of falsehood if he believed himself to be something great. And therefore, withdrawing from himself, he fails in himself, and places his being, his life, and his power in God alone. Secondly, this disposition arises from hope of acquiring greater grace, because when a man through humility fails in himself, he comes nearer to the grace of God. Thirdly, the disposition of this humility takes its beginning from the love of God, and by continuing in it receives increase. For whoever perfectly loves God seeks nothing in all things except his honor, nor does he know how to exalt himself in anything, but for God’s sake desires to be subject to all. Therefore the more he is cast down by reproaches and injuries, the more joyfully he rejoices in the Lord. He rejoices that he is wretched, so that in himself he may proclaim the Lord glorious. Whoever truly loves his Lord seeks nothing else but his glory.

From what we have said it is clear that the perfect charity promised to those who ascend through the degrees of humility is displayed in this seventh degree. For the other five degrees that follow in the Rule add nothing to the perfection of the inner man who exists in the seventh degree, but rather compose outward things so that they may not dissipate the inner man. Finally, from the seventh degree we could set up a certain new ascent of humility, and in them lift all the other degrees higher. For filial fear resides more fervently in him who can make wider progress than others.

Now that the ascents of the heart up to the degree of charity have been known, let the cenobite consider with what zeal, what effort, and what perseverance he ought to exercise himself in these things, so that he may reach this seventh degree of love. But whoever does not always strive to advance in these degrees of humility should know that he sins against the Rule; and unless by repentance he recovers his holy striving, he incurs the sentence of damnation. For thus the Rule says: “But if at any time he has done otherwise, let him know that he is to be condemned by him whom he mocks.” If, then, anyone who makes less progress in religion is believed guilty before the divine judgment, when he abandons the effort to advance, what else does he deserve to receive but the sentence of damnation? For where the Rule gives an account even of lesser progress among those striving to advance, monks who despise every effort to advance are without doubt condemned by the sentence of the judge. Therefore, if you do not wish to incur the danger of damnation, take care always to keep the effort of advancing under the Rule.

Since we have said that the other five degrees of humility pertain to the guarding of the inner man, let us also explain them briefly. For the monk who neglects to compose his outward conduct according to the Rule will not stand well composed in inward things. For just as a body stripped of clothing is corrupted, so humility without conduct is emptied.

Therefore the eighth degree of humility is set forth in the Rule thus: if a monk does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders encourage. In this degree, singularity in outward conduct contrary to the Rule is forbidden to monks; but inward singularity of greater charity and humility is forbidden to no one. Therefore let no one prefer his own inventions to the holy Rule; let no one set his own customs before the examples of the elders, since standing in the seventh degree is not enough for one who does not keep the common rule.

The ninth degree of humility follows from the Rule, by which excessive talkativeness is forbidden. It is fitting for monks to keep silence, especially while one sits among the elders. And indeed, one who speaks without being asked is deservedly regarded as a fool.

The tenth degree of humility forbids readiness to laugh and levity; whoever delights in laughter is shown to be foolish and a stranger to the fear of the Lord.

The eleventh degree of humility commands modesty and dignity in a monk, so that, when opportunity and permission to speak are granted him, he may speak with humble seriousness, without laughter, and as befits a monk. Let a monk’s speech be rare, brief, and reasonable, because it is not fitting for him to say useless things who wishes to please the Most High.

The twelfth degree of humility teaches a monk to compose the outward man, in appearance and bearing, from a humble heart, and to show by outward conduct also that he is devout within. And although this degree is last in the order of all of them, nevertheless in practice it begins to make progress and is first. Therefore Bernard, describing these twelve degrees of humility, begins from this one and, ascending to the first, descends, so to speak, in order. For no one easily makes inward progress toward compunction of heart and fear of the Lord who does not compose his outward behavior.

On the fitting of the powers of the soul for entry into the third region. Article six.

When, through the degrees of humility, the powers of the soul, especially of the inner man, have been purified, firmly founded, and reformed, he now says that it is very necessary for monks to be more devoutly fitted for entry into the third region. This diligence in striving toward higher things is necessary for cenobites, as is said, because where the effort to make progress is laid aside, acquired virtue is wholly dissipated.

No one is permitted to stand still in this second region, but we are all commanded to ascend to the third by continual effort. For indeed this continual movement casts all the slothful and lukewarm back into the first region, that of the flesh; but it gently impels the humble, fervent with desire, always toward the third, without violence. Therefore whoever has deserved, through humility, to obtain from the Lord the power and reformation of his soul is now very near the third region, that of the spirit. In order that he may be able to enter it with strength, it is necessary that he most diligently fit the powers of his soul and compose them for their individual operations. The intellect is said to be rightly fitted for entry into the third region when it is enlightened to know the highest truth according to its capacity. The memory is composed for the same thing when it is fully absorbed in holding and cherishing the highest truth. And if the will is disposed to love the highest good, which is God, it is well fitted for entry into the spirit.

But in order that a cenobite may be able to attain the purification of the intellectual powers, it is necessary that, withdrawn from the world, the mind, pacified from every inward and outward disturbance, should rest, so that it may remain buried in the bosom of divine love and never withdraw from the sweetness of inward union. This rest of mind is reached by four degrees, which are rooted in good will in four ways.

The first degree of good will sets [unclear] before virtue.

which is called right will. For the soul which, consenting to the law of God, is subjected to God through a right will, even if it still seems weak, is being set in order for the passage to virtue. With the flesh resisting, virtue is perfected; and that the will is right is proved by the vehemence of the spirit. Often, however, a will is called right and good even when it is found to be less strong. The good which it loves it cannot always accomplish; the evil which it hates it grieves that through weakness it has committed. By the weakness of the flesh it is very near the region of infirmity, yet by the uprightness of its intention and by the effort to advance it is continually kindled toward the liberty of the spirit. For the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling depresses the sense that thinks on many things. O who could describe this battle between spirit and flesh, where the spirit itself desires to subdue the flesh to itself through a right will, and the weak flesh always resists the spirit through contrary desires?
