The second degree is a will strong in uprightness, so that it both firmly flees the evil which it hates, against the assault of the flesh, and strongly lays hold of the good which it loves by doing it, even with labor.

The third degree is a devout will, by which the mind, with enlarged heart, embraces the way of God’s commandments and delights in them as in all riches. For a will does not long remain strong if it has not been devout in the commandments of God.

The fourth degree is a full will, inasmuch as it does not divide its powers at all, but wholly stretches itself out continually toward its God through the denial of all things. For this degree three things are necessary, so that the good will in us may be made full.

The first is full denial of oneself, since a will is proved still to be weak if it is not mortified through complete denial of itself.

The second thing required for a full good will is said to be perfect resignation; if anyone truly desires to apprehend it, let him fervently ascend the third degree of humility.

The third member necessary for the fourth degree of good will is called the total extension of the will into God. Through it the soul, moved toward divine love and sweetly burning, is in a certain way transformed into that same love, and is frequently admitted into the third region.

Finally, this transformation into divine love, according to Bernard’s judgment, is love, affection, adhesion, union, charity, and enjoyment. No one can attain it unless he has learned to mortify all his affections in the fervor of the spirit. For the spirit of a good will, having the heart lifted upward into God, is called a perfect will, and by it the soul is joined to most sweet God in covenant. Therefore in these degrees of good will the faithful monk must direct his effort upward without interruption, and with prudent zeal always examine how much he advances or falls short. For Saint Bernard says: Just as he who remains in a vicious will is condemned, so he who does not strive to advance in higher things is blameworthy. For where the effort to advance is laid aside, one enters upon the dangers of descending.

On the Example of All the Things Said Above, from Experimental Certainty Article VII Although a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, nevertheless each person can, by diligently examining his conscience, recognize what he ought to think about the condition of his state. What sort of person each one lies hidden within, before himself, the testimony of his own knowledge makes manifest. Therefore, so that a monk may be able clearly to discern the condition of his state, he must, according to John of Kastl, observe three things in his conscience as a rule; without these no one becomes a good Christian, and no one is judged a good man or monk.

The first, then, which is required for a good man and for the testimony of a good conscience, is that no mortal sin lie hidden in the conscience. For the mind which is polluted by the guilt of mortal sin has the testimony of an evil state of conscience.

Therefore a monk must diligently examine himself and purge himself of his committed faults according to the ordinance of the Church. But he who, on examining himself, by his own knowledge finds his conscience clean from mortal sin, should offer humble praises to God; yet he should not neglect to subject himself to the following examination.

The second thing, likewise necessary for a good man, is to direct his intention chiefly to God in all works, and to order all things, according to his powers, to his praise and honor. But if, because the multitude and variety of works hinders him, a man cannot always actually keep God before his eyes, let him at least conform his habitual intention of living according to God’s most gracious will to this desire.

The third is that in all things he should obey God, holy mother Church, and his superiors, and not depart from the path of right and enlightened reason, since whoever despises this threefold obedience has denied the faith. It is therefore necessary to show obedience in due order to these three according to the reasons of their institution, so that the life of monks may remain blameless in their actions, without fear.

These three things, possessed with humble sincerity, make a good man and show the state of a conscience that hopes well in the Lord. But a man who lacks one of these is not perfectly good, even if he seems to be good. Yet if, repenting of his sins, he is able from then on to fulfill these three things, he is now made good and pleasing to God, however evil he may previously have been. Furthermore, for a good religious or spiritual man to be born from a good man, three other things are required, according to the lord of Castellum.

The first thing required for making a good religious is that purity of heart be cleansed from every rivalry or incitement of the flesh through the pursuit of discipline. This purity is never acquired better than when the world, with all its things, is despised.

The second thing by which a good man is made a good religious is called spiritual freedom in God. Once the phantasms of all things have been shut out, the soul can raise itself, unencumbered, upward to God in all its exercises, and continually lift itself without hindrance in thanksgiving with devout prayers.

In the third way a good man is made spiritually good when, through the desires of love, the spirit is joined to God by certain great bonds. The last two things make our cenobite spiritual and introduce him to the citizens of the third region of the enclosures. Therefore whoever wishes to have good confidence from the testimony of his conscience should humbly strive to exercise himself in the things set forth, because no one prudently presumes upon security when danger is not avoided. And what is so dangerous as always to live in negligence and sins, and to refuse to amend committed errors? The confidence of the just, arising from the testimony of a good conscience, is always excellent, and continually subject to God in humble service. But the impious and sinners, corrupted by their evil actions, raise themselves up against God and do not trust in the testimony of conscience, but rather presume vainly.

There follow the seven roots of divine fear, which are laid as a foundation in the first degree of humility.

Since this second region principally instructs the cenobite, in order, through the degrees of humility proceeding from the fear of God, it is necessary for him to know clearly the roots of that fear, if he wishes to arrive, by ascending, at the love of God. Therefore, so that we may be able to construct this spiritual house to perfection, we must set those roots in order in the foundation. We did not arrange them in the first degree of humility for this reason: lest, in speaking in order, we should confuse the reader by excessive length. There are therefore seven roots of the fear of God, through which the cenobite is led to compunction and, by advancing in true humility, is more strongly rooted.

The first root of fear, of the love of God, is intense meditation.

The less the incomprehensible divine majesty can be grasped, the more curiously it is investigated by man. For the prophet says: “Truly you are a hidden God.” Meditation on divine perfection begets wonder; wonder causes reverence; from reverence arises fear of majesty, and from fear worship grows.

But the meditation of the highest goodness is divided, according to our purpose, into seven parts, which are not unfittingly adapted to the seven days of the week, or also to the seven canonical hours. And although that highest and most perfect goodness abundantly suffices for us as material for meditation, yet, because it belongs to few to be able to ascend to invisible things without visible ones, we wish to raise the minds of the weak through things known to things unknown. For the holy apostle says: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; his everlasting power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse.”

First, therefore, the wondrous power of God is praiseworthy in the principal work of creation, since he, who was able to bring all things forth from nothing, created things so great, so solid, so varied, and so noble by his will alone. From this consideration arises wonder at the divine power, through which man is moved to the fear of God.

Second, the provident wisdom of God is praiseworthy, because, knowing all things, he orders the universe, and governs by his providence all things that he has created. He knows all things, understands all things; by his counsel he disposes all things; by his command he encloses all things. As a certain lover of the wisdom of the world says: God is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. He is within all things and is not enclosed; outside all things and not excluded; beneath all things and not oppressed; above all things and not borne up. He includes all things, and because he is wholly everywhere, he is confined in no place; great and immeasurable, he is bounded by no quantity. He orders all things as he wills; stable in himself, always unmoved, he changes the vicissitudes of things; good, without passion of mind, he mercifully prepares eternal things for merits; angered without disturbance, he condemns the unjust. Great without magnitude, immeasurable without quantity, he has set bounds to things; governing the world, he disposes all things.

Third, the merciful clemency of God is praiseworthy in our redemption, because he so mercifully restored man, whom he had made in his own image and who had fallen so miserably into the pit of damnation. O what shall I render to the highest and incomprehensible majesty, I, a little worm, indeed nothing compared with my maker, who, when I did not exist, created me by his power, and, when I had perished, being made man for my sake and dying on the cross, redeemed me? What shall I repay you, mediator of God and men, Jesus, savior of the world, who, though you are the high and inestimable God, became man for my sake, most vile as I am, and willed to undergo things so vile and unworthy? Behold, my heart speaks to you; all my inward parts are bowed toward you, since no voice can express what you inwardly give your faithful to feel in their hearts concerning your most innocent Passion.

Fourth, in the work of our justification the kind patience of God is praiseworthy, because he not only mercifully bears with sinners, but even calls those who are to be justified to penance by promised eternal joys. Who could sufficiently praise this most indulgent clemency of the Father, who so mercifully justifies sinners returning to him, grants after a fall the grace of meriting, arranges many occasions for living well, supplies his sacraments to the penitent as certain vessels of grace? Finally, for compunction, instruction, consolation, and the working of grace, he pours the Holy Spirit into his faithful, making friends and sons out of enemies. He does not consider what sort of sinner a man was before; he seeks only that henceforth he remain faithful to him. Great is the clemency of divine compassion, which so mercifully receives the penitent to pardon, and even promises them great rewards after guilt.

Fifth, the deep justice of God is praiseworthy in the damnation of the reprobate, because he permits no evil to pass unpunished, depriving the sinner of the good which, in sinning, the fool does not fear to lose. Finally, to speak in our manner, the highest cleanness of God is shown praiseworthy in this: that it abominates all sin and vice like a putrid corpse. We also recognize that his wisdom is praiseworthy in the damnation of the wicked, drawing good things even from evils for himself [unclear].

he compels them to serve in punishment, who, in guilt, are unwilling to be subject to justice when they sin against it.

Sixth, the generous munificence of God is praiseworthy in the glorification of the blessed, since he rewards his few elect, according to their merit, with so ineffable a recompense, and grants them so immortal a gift with the holy angels.

Seventh, the incomprehensible excellence of God is praiseworthy in himself: he orders all things according to his providence, and in himself remains most tranquil, immovable by everlasting motion or by time. The seventh contemplation of this consideration belongs to the Sabbath of eternal happiness, in which there is no longer the laborious activity of this life, but the blessedness of a happy, eternal dwelling and rest. For just as God, the creator of all things, is read to have completed all his work and rested on the seventh day, so not work, but eternal rest, will be laid upon the just in the heavenly Sabbath. Therefore, if we desire happily to come to those heavenly mansions, let us rest in God alone, in whom the rational creature is perfected by resting; and, once perfected through the attachment of love, it rejoices with the Lord in ineffable union and joy. Henceforth let pure devotion seek nothing outside God for praising God, since God himself, almighty, perfect, and most wise, is sufficient to all as the matter of his praise, and exceeds every praise by his infinite perfections. For Scripture says: “Praise the Lord as much as you can; he will still surpass it.” For he is greater than all praise; and therefore he is to be praised by us most humbly rather in himself and for his own sake than from creatures.

From the foregoing considerations there arises a manifold and varied affection of devotion toward God, through which a worthier effect of prayer is also generated according to the desire of the affection. For when the meditation of the heart is taken up concerning the majesty or power of God, reverent wonder is produced. But when we begin to meditate on his unspeakable wisdom, we accuse ourselves within ourselves of our foolish imperfection. So, in consequence, from the consideration of God’s mercy hope of pardon is taken up; from his patience love of heart is generated; from justice humility is born; from meditation on his munificence, gratitude. For just as a fire that has been kindled grows in size according to the quality of the wood, so, according to varied meditations on God, the ardor of devotion rises up in prayers among those who love God.

On the meditation of our reparation in the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The second root of the fear and love of God is placed in meditation on our redemption, which is generated through diligent exercise in the life, conduct, teaching, and Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. Among all meditations, we believe none to be more useful to us than this, in which we know that our salvation and the sum of eternal happiness are contained. And note that the Passion of the Lord, as to its legal proceeding, was unjust; as to its manner, shameful; as to its pain, bitter; and as to its effect, fruitful; and therefore it must always be kept in memory.

First, as to its legal proceeding, it was unjust, because he who was born of a virgin neither contracted sin nor committed it, nor was deceit found in his mouth. For death is inflicted on us for sin; but he could not justly die, because he was always just and innocent, without any sin. Finally, he was killed contrary to human law, if a sentence of death is passed upon a man neither confessed nor convicted of a crime. For he was accused before Pilate the governor on three counts: that, calling himself a king, he forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar; third, that he made himself the Son of God. The Gospel speaks of the first two, and the accusation is shown to be false. For concerning the first, the contrary was plainly established, since Christ said that his kingdom was not earthly. The falsity of the second also did not escape Pilate, because he knew that Jesus had commanded that the things that were Caesar’s should be given to Caesar. When questioned by the governor about the third, he was silent, because Pilate [unclear] to hear the divine generation.

He was unworthy even of Jesus’ human birth [unclear].

His Passion was also contrary to custom, because it received no delay of time. According to custom he is not put in prison; nothing is deliberated in his case. Instead, once captured, he is immediately handed over to the judge to be condemned to death; scourged, spat upon, afflicted with many injuries, blows, and mockeries, he is nailed to the cross.

Third, it was contrary to the law of nature, and procured by the obstinate hatred of the heart. For nature forbids cruelty against the dead, and shudders to tear a slain body with new wounds. For our Redeemer, dead upon the cross, is pierced with a lance; and, contrary to the law of nature, the departed one is wounded by the impious.

Second, the Passion of Christ is said to have been ignominious in its manner, for the six causes that follow. First, because of the paltry price: the blood of incomparable worth is sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver, for which no one would deign to sell his little donkey. Second, because of the ignominious office: filled with wounds and half dead, he is compelled to carry his own cross, something found to have been done to no robber. Third, because of the unworthy place: he is crucified outside the city, in the place of Calvary, where robbers and wicked murderers are punished for their deserts. Fourth, because of the ignominious punishment: he is hung naked upon the cross, a penalty owed only to robbers and wicked men. Indeed, as Scripture says, the Redeemer of the world was condemned to a most shameful death. Fifth, because of the ignominious mockery: naked before the whole multitude he is hung upon the cross, and is blasphemed by all as though he were a fool and a madman. Of this the psalmist says: “All the day my shame is before me.” Sixth, because of the ignominious company: numbered with the wicked, he is hung in the midst of robbers.

What are you doing now, O Christian soul? Behold, your Savior hangs in the middle between robbers, and you are not afraid to sit in the first places in council?

Third, the most holy Passion was most bitter with regard to pain, for seven reasons. First, because of the delicate and lively nature of his flesh, which in its natural constitution was the best; therefore it was grievously afflicted in the oppression of pain. For delicate flesh suffers more than flesh coarse by natural condition. Since, then, the flesh of Christ was fine and delicate, in the garden it gave forth a bloody sweat. Second, because of the character of those who killed him: for Christ was not killed by strangers, but by his own kinsmen and closest people, as he had earlier complained through the prophet: “My people, what have I done to you?” For one suffers more tolerably from strangers and enemies than from one’s own people, from whom at least friends by nearness of blood feel compassion. Third, because of the bitterness of the Passion: he is afflicted most in those places where pain is felt more strongly because of the nerves. For raised upon the cross, he is fastened by hands and feet; the Lord of the universe is given gall and vinegar to drink. For the psalmist says of him: “They have dug my hands and my feet; they have numbered all my bones.”

Who could conceive in his mind the pain of your most holy heart, O good Jesus, when they began so cruelly to pierce your most pure hands and feet? Would that my soul may always show itself grateful to you; would that the remembrance of your most holy Passion may never depart from my memory. I shall easily be able to obtain from you the effect of my prayers if I have taken care to delight without interruption in the exercise of your Passion. Let each one think what he can: I prefer the memory of your Passion to all exercises, through which I trust that in my prayers I shall receive whatever accords with salvation.

Fourth, because of the long duration, the Passion of Christ was most bitter: from the hour of his captivity up to his death he was always in most bitter torment. “All the day,” he says, “I went about sorrowful, and there is no soundness in my flesh.” Fifth, because of the universality of the Passion: for in whatever ways Christ could suffer, he suffered singularly. For he suffers in his reputation, because, falsely accused, he is blasphemed by the impious. He also suffers in his possessions, because, naked and stripped, he is hung upon the wood.

whose garments are divided by lot among the soldiers. He suffers in his soul, because, feeling beforehand the bitterness of the Passion, he was sorrowful even unto death. He suffered in his whole body, because from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no soundness in him. He suffers in his friends, because he is betrayed by a disciple and, deserted by all, is even publicly denied by Peter. He is afflicted also in compassion for his mother, whose most holy soul is remembered as having been pierced by the sword of grief. He suffered much from ingratitude, because he foresaw that the death which he underwent in compassion for all would be lost in the case of many reprobates. Finally, he suffered in all his senses, as we are taught from the Gospel. He suffers in his eyes, because, with many tears poured out, they are covered with a cloth. He suffers in his hearing, when he is mocked, reviled, and blasphemed with many insults and abuses. He suffers in his smell, because he is defiled with the most foul spittle of the Jews. He suffers in his touch, because he is tortured in every member of his body. He suffers in his taste, because, thirsting, he is given gall and vinegar to drink.

Sixth, because of the cause of the Passion, which was solely the envy of the Jews, since he suffered wholly without guilt. For indeed, whoever suffers unjustly is tormented all the more in his soul. But the innocent Son of God dies for our sins; he is tormented for our crimes, as is read in Isaiah: “Truly he himself bore our infirmities.”

Seventh, because of the lack of every consolation, since Christ found no one to console him in his Passion. For he says in the Psalm: “You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery.” Indeed, his acquaintances stood far off.

Fourth, the Passion of Christ was most fruitful in its effect, which is to be considered principally in three things: first, the remission of sins; second, the bestowal of grace; third, the showing forth of glory. And these three things are indicated by the title fastened to the cross, which, as the Evangelist says, contained the cause of Jesus’ Passion: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” For “Jesus,” saving sinners, refers to the first; “of Nazareth,” that is, conferring grace, refers to the second; “King of the Jews,” showing the heavenly kingdom to those who confess him, refers to the third.

Moreover, in this second root we have arranged meditations on the Passion of the Lord for the several hours of the seven days of the week; we have placed them after the end of the third section for this reason, lest, by setting them down in order here, we should disturb this place with their excessive abundance. For the things we have now set out seem to pertain rather to readings than to meditation; therefore we postpone them.

On Meditation on the Benefits of God The third root of divine fear and love lies in meditation on the benefits of God, through which one comes to the grace of devotion. Indeed, the beginning of devotion is placed in meditation on the benefits of God, from which love is generated by memory. Its middle is progress in that meditation itself, when one desires nothing above all things except to please God, from whom he knows that he has been anticipated by many benefits without any merit of his own. Its end, however, is to love God above all things with burning desire and the pure fervor of the mind, and to long to cling continually to him alone without any intermediary.

And since the merciful God has bestowed many things specially on each one of us, yet because we are writing these our symbols not for one person but for many, we must briefly place before them not the particular benefits given to individuals, but the general benefits common to all. Therefore we comprehend the chief ones under the number seven, so that through the seven days of the week, or even in the canonical hours themselves, we may have material ready each day for meditation. But if anyone, through the elevation of his mind, has experience in higher things concerning God, let him not seek the spoils of one still a novice. But whoever, because of the weakness of his mind, cannot ascend to that supreme summit of contemplation should strive to exercise himself more fervently in these meditations on the benefits of God, so that, while he diligently continues in lower things, purified and stronger, he may ascend to higher things.

Therefore let the devout monk remember what he has received from the Lord God, so that he may be able to show himself grateful. Let him give back to God what he has received, if he longs to be good. For first God gave us body and soul with [unclear].

with his adornments, and those whom he made intellectual beings in his own image he also mercifully called to the heavenly kingdoms. What more could he have given us, he who, when we had been created and were not, gave himself? But what can we render to our Creator, since by our deserts we are sinners and weak? Let us render what we are; let us render what we owe: faithful service, for the body which we have received from the Lord, and sincere love for the soul, by which we were created in the image of God. Thus the prophet admonishes us in the psalm: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling.” Serve faithfully; love reverently. On the part of the body, offer faithful service to your Creator; on the part of the soul, love him with all your strength. Serve him, because he is powerful and great among lords; love him, because he is good. His power is shown in your creation; his goodness is made manifest in your restoration. For since he created you, when you were not, by his power, he deserves faithful service; since he restored the fallen by his goodness, he deserves the affection of sincere love. Truly he is our father through love; he is Lord through incomprehensible power.

Secondly, he gave us faith with the sacraments; for just as he created us without our will, so he called us to faith without our merit. For Christ says to his disciples in the holy Gospel: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” Through faith the Christian soul is led back to its beginning; the sacraments renew it. Therefore, incorporated into Christ through faith and the sacraments which he gave, we are bound to cleave to him forever, and to remain continually in his holy covenant. For in baptism we renounced the devil and all his pomps; we promised that we would forever adhere to Christ, when, lifting us from the sacred font, our sponsors set us before the Lord in the faith of our parents. Let us therefore always say from the heart with the prophet: “It is good for me to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord God.”

Thirdly, almighty God gave us the art of uprightness and the teachings of truth. For these we are bound to our Creator in faithful performance and in perpetual service without deceit.

Therefore we are commanded first of all to do everything for the praise of God, and in all that we do to raise our intention principally toward that good. For only a good intention in God distinguishes works; only love makes them fruitful. Behold, nature has bestowed on us the art of praising God; moreover, he has given us the teachings of salvation through the law; he requires from us praise and love above all things. Let us therefore exercise, for the honor of God, the skills entrusted to us, and let the pure eye of intention be formed through the teaching of the law.

Fourthly, the merciful Father bestowed on us the world with its necessary elements; for these he requires from us due contemplation of himself in sincerity. Whatever we behold in this world ought to lead us to the remembrance of God, and continually summon us to love its Creator above all things. Hence Bernard, trained in sacred things, says: The whole and true lover of God, wherever he turns, has a reminder of his familiar Creator; he uses things as a mirror, and from creatures is lifted up to the Creator by thinking thus about each one: If these things that are created in time, changed, and passing away seem good, beautiful, and sweet, what goodness, beauty, and sweetness does their author, God himself, possess, who remains eternal and has reserved incomparably better things for his own? By this consideration the devout person looks upon all people with the simple eye of the mind, as though in the likeness of God’s image, and does not curiously attend to whether the form of the body is pleasing or displeasing. In this he considers not what he sees outwardly, but the creature made in God’s image, whom he knows to be a sharer in eternal happiness.

Fifthly, the Son of God offered himself in torments for us, and redeemed us, lost as we were, from the destruction of perpetual death by his own blood. We are commanded to offer him a loving imitation of our Savior’s charity, if we desire to reach his kingdom. For the prince of the apostles says to the faithful: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps.” What shall I render to you, O good Jesus, for your benefits to me, so many, so great, so immeasurable?

I shall sympathize in heart and cooperate in deed; I shall imitate you in the affections of the mind as far as I can.

Sixth, the Creator has bestowed on us time for meriting eternal life, and has given the necessary nourishment of the body. Here too we are debtors to ourselves, since in this time we owe ourselves the acquisition of merit. Why then do we spend the days of salvation so negligently and without the fruit of merit, when we have nothing more precious than time? Behold, in this brief time we can merit the joys of eternal happiness, and yet we neglect to do every good thing. Woe to us, foolish and mad, who esteem nothing in this world more precious than time, and yet are accustomed to spend nothing more cheaply. For now this acceptable time is granted to us; now the days of salvation are bestowed, in which we ought to devote ourselves to holy works with the greatest fervor, and always keep the hour of death before our eyes.

Seventh, God has set heaven before us all, filled with joys, and has promised himself, with all things contained in it, as our reward. For this munificence of our Savior we ought to devote ourselves to holy works of mercy, and show ourselves imitators of God as far as our strength allows. The Lord exhorts us to this in the holy Gospels: “Be merciful, just as your Father God is merciful.” Likewise at the end of the world, when the day of judgment comes, the merciful, as the Lord himself promises, will go into eternal life, because whoever has shown mercy will obtain mercy. And lest anyone say to me, “As a monk I can bestow mercy on no one, since my religious state permits me to possess absolutely nothing,” we should know that among the necessary works of mercy, spiritual works are more important. If, as a monk, you wish to be merciful, pray to God for the wretched; impart saving doctrine to the ignorant.

The sum, then, of meditation on benefits rests on three exercises, in which it is principally contained. In the first, we ought to attribute all things to God, not to ourselves; in the second, by remembering God’s benefits, we ought to exercise ourselves in the pursuit of love; in the third, we ought always to give thanks from a pure heart for benefits received. But if by these exercises concerning benefits we wish to kindle our heart to the love of God, we ought to consider six conditions in the Lord’s gifts. First, consider that the gift of God is utterly noble; second, that it is especially fruitful and useful to you; third, that it is varied, manifold, and very frequently repeated. These three consider the gift as ordered in itself; the two that follow regard the person of the giver; the last marks the condition of the receiver. Fourth, therefore, consider the great affection of the giver toward you; fifth, his inestimable dignity; sixth, that you, the receiver, are lowly and contemptible, receiving great things from the greatest, and unworthy of all things. From these considerations of benefits, the love of God is accustomed to arise in the mind of the devout person, and, advancing by fixed degrees, to lift the spirit to contemplation.

On knowledge of oneself.

The fourth root producing divine love is called knowledge of oneself, very useful if it is referred to the preceding things. For if it is brought back to the mind in consideration how great a Lord has done such great things for us who are so little, we shall recognize that we are unworthy, vile, and wholly undeserving of all things. Four things ought to lead a person to knowledge of himself; from consideration of them we are especially fittingly moved to love God.

First, then, let the faithful person consider the beginning of his creation, and he will find that, when he did not exist, he was created from the goodness of God alone. Who could ask God, when no one existed? That highest, utterly ineffable good, O man, made you to his image when you did not exist; from goodness alone he made you a sharer in his goodness. What did you deserve when you did not exist? Or what advantage could your condition bring to almighty God, who, always subsisting unchangeably in himself, admits no accident? Nothing is new to God; nothing can be old to the highest and unchangeable good. He is always [unclear].

God created you by his goodness, not because your creation was necessary to him, but because it was useful to you alone. Whoever considers this goodness of God with intent meditation rightly praises his creator.

Second, lest you be lifted up into pride, O man, consider the vileness of your condition: you were made from the mud of the earth, and after a little while, consumed by worms, you will return to the dust of the earth. Why then are you proud, earth and ashes? Your conception has guilt, your birth misery, your life punishment, your dissolution the anguish of death. For man, born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries; and he is then most miserable when he does not recognize himself as miserable in the flesh.

Third, consider the origin of your conception, and you will find your soul stained with the foulness of original sin. For we are born children of God’s wrath; but by the grace of baptism, in the blood of Christ Jesus, we are cleansed from the original stain. Through this consideration we rightly love our Savior, by whose mercy we have been cleansed from the original stain.

Fourth, faithful soul, consider how very foolish and [unclear] you are when you repeat your ways in the act of sin: you, who have presented yourself as an adulteress to Christ your bridegroom, though he joined you to himself by his own blood, wholly unstained. What are you doing, O wretched one? Why do you desert your most loving bridegroom? Or why, foolish one, do you withdraw from your beginning? Know that you have been placed in the flesh, not so that you should yield to vicious and concupiscent impulses, but rather so that you should resist their prompt command. For as often as you hand yourself over to the disordered motions of the flesh, contrary to divine rectitude, by dissembling your [unclear], so often, turned away from the good, you show yourself an adulteress to your bridegroom. Beware, beware, O soul redeemed by the blood of Christ, lest love of the flesh deceive you; for just as the first man, deceived by love of his companion, the woman, fell into death, so every soul that consents to the pleasures of its flesh shamefully withdraws from its beginning, which is God. But alas, wretched soul, where have you fallen? You have dwelt in a foreign land; you have been defiled with the dead; you have been counted with those who go down into hell. You have forsaken the fountain of wisdom; you have sought a backward path, adultery.

But hear my counsel, and return as quickly as possible to the guide of your youth, Jesus. Submit yourself wholly to him in humility. He is merciful; he will gladly receive you when you return to him, forgive your sins, and, if you ask, bestow the grace of his love. But you must withdraw from the affections of the flesh if you desire to come into the sight of your Savior. Therefore, if you turn to Jesus, turn in truth, because supreme Truth can love only what is true.

There is also another mode of self-knowledge, which is taken up with respect to God whenever one thinks upon the incomparable comparison between God and man. Concerning this mode Bernard, renowned in contemplation, says: “The mode of human imperfection is never better perceived than in the light of God’s countenance and the mirror of divine vision. For there one who is more in the day, and sees more clearly what is lacking in himself, amends day by day through likeness whatever he has lost through unlikeness, drawing near to him by likeness from whom he has been made far off by unlikeness.” Let us therefore raise the gaze of the mind to the most bright mirror of divine perfection; let us submit our affection to that unchangeable good, so that in God’s wisdom we may be able to perceive our foolishness, and in his power consider our weakness.

On Keeping the Memory of One’s Sins Root Six The fifth root of the fear of God is the memory of sins, and the foulness of sin itself often pondered. For anyone who truly understands the ugliness of mortal sin always dreads the pit of this evil. But so that you may in some measure recognize the gravity of sin, you must consider the seven things that follow.

First, then, consider the beauty of God’s justice, to which sin is wholly contrary, and for that reason must be fled above all. For through sin the soul turns utterly away from the highest good, and the love that is naturally in it toward its beginning is changed into hatred.

For as all good things are from the first Good, so every love, toward whatever good it is borne, is naturally kindled by that same Good. For since our love cannot rest in any goods as in its end, it has as its end, where it is to rest, the same Good that it had also as its beginning. Therefore, as often as sin is committed against the beauty of God’s justice, the soul is separated from its own beginning. For since God is charity, he requires love in the soul; being peace, he requires peace; he loves what is like himself and hates what is unlike.

Second, consider the enormity of sin, and carefully weigh how greatly its foulness displeases God. Behold, because of pride the just God cast the most noble angel Lucifer out of heaven, and condemned him with his accomplices to the burning of eternal fire. He compelled our first parents, Adam and Eve, to leave paradise because of disobedience, and by a just judgment condemned the whole human race, in their crime, to the sentence of a twofold death. Finally, let us review the whole history of the Old and New Testament, and we shall find that what was rashly committed against God’s justice was often severely punished by that justice. Therefore the gravity of the crime is easily known if the severity of the vengeance that followed is considered.

Third, consider that grave scandal arises from sin, especially when one sins before others. For whoever by his own evil example provokes someone to sin shows himself to be an adversary of God. For God, in his mercy, has willed to save the souls redeemed by the blood of his only-begotten Son; but this man, through evil example, desires to destroy them out of aversion from God. Sin that gives scandal is truly said, with respect to guilt, to be most grave for this reason: because, as we have said, it is opposed to God. But if the one who gives occasion for harm is to be thought to have done harm, the sinner subjects himself to as many sentences of death as there are people whom he has caused by his evil example to fall into mortal crime. For Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Woe to the man through whom scandal comes.” And again he says: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it is expedient for him that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.” True repentance is rare in one who scandalizes the little ones, because he neglects to restore another’s loss and by no means reaches the fruits of saving repentance.

Fourth, consider the negligence of your ungrateful heart, because, created in the image of God, you ought to have loved your maker above all things, yet you dishonor him in many ways by your sins. To Christ, the Son of God, by whose blood you were redeemed, you ought to offer continual service of love; but you do not fear to love your flesh more than Jesus your Savior. You ought daily, with a compassionate soul, to revolve his most holy passion in your mind; and you are accustomed to think of nothing less than that. Adopted among the children of God by his merciful calling, you ought to have shown yourself an imitator worthy of the heavenly vocation; and still you do not fear to lie in the lowest things. And why do I say much? Behold: you, marked with the Holy Spirit, counted among the angels, are called to the inheritance of the children of God, are invited by all the saints to the feasts of paradise, and daily partake of the body and blood of our Savior Jesus Christ; and yet you do not keep the commandments of God and the rule that you promised, so that you might be blessed. Examine your conscience diligently, therefore, and you will find that there are many good things you ought to do and omit, and many evil things you ought to omit and instead commit against God’s good pleasure.

Fifth, consider whom you offend by sinning: not a man, but God; not a creature, but the Creator. Great is he against whom you have sinned, and immeasurable, terrible, and glorious; at his majesty the angels tremble, and at his power all the hosts of heaven marvel. To the supreme and unchangeable Good, God, the beginning and end of every creature, the rational spirit ought to offer love and the desire of cleaving beyond human understanding; it ought truly to raise itself with its whole being to touch that one Good as its own center, all phantasms despised, more highly; and it can lift itself up to him so much the more easily [unclear].

leaving all other things, he has striven to unite himself to himself. For by the power of that one itself union is made; nor are things more alike more easily united to one another for any other reason than because in quality they are one. Therefore the soul is then most rightly said to be united with the one principle of things itself, when, having itself become most fully one within itself, it is separated from all multiplicity and, above all imagination, reason, and understanding, its own unity alone comes forth, enjoying through loving affection the unity of God, joining its center, so to speak, with the center of the universe. But when the human soul itself, suffering badly through the contagion, as it were, of the flesh, is turned toward any animal passions, then that very unity is badly changed into a multiplicity contrary to the one alone; it becomes as far removed from its principle as it has been divided from itself. The soul itself contracts great difficulty in returning to that one ineffable divine thing whenever, confused in itself, it falls through sin into apostasy. Think now how great and ineffable he is against whose honor sin is committed; and since you are utterly unable to understand the greatness of his majesty, learn humbly to fear his power.

Sixth, consider what you have lost by sinning, so that the recognized greatness of the loss may hasten penitence and restore through tears what was lost. What then, wretched man, have you lost by sinning? Hear what you have lost. Made like to God by grace, higher than the angels, a member of Christ, and an heir of eternal happiness, you had been chosen; you ought to have lived and rejoiced without end in the good things of the Lord with all the saints. But what happened when you sinned? You were compared to senseless beasts, and made like them. Since you were in honor and did not wish to understand, you abandoned the fountain of life; by sinning you became a companion and member of the devil, a whore of Antichrist, an heir of hell. You abandoned life; you chose everlasting death. If you fear the sentence, change your will, and you will find forgiveness.

Seventh, consider what you have deserved by sinning; for if eternal death is inflicted for one sin, think what a man deserves who has committed many, not to say innumerable, sins. For the soul that has sinned shall itself die. By one mortal sin you have deserved to be a companion of the devil without end, to be deprived of all the joys of heaven, and to be burned forever in the fires of hell. These are the rewards that sin has brought you; these are the gifts it has promised.

Therefore from these seven considerations make a plaster for the wounded soul; take up for yourself the spur of compunction, so that you may come to the root of fear. But on that account do not put it off from day to day, since he who receives the humble confession of the penitent has not promised tomorrow to the one who delays. For where speed finds pardon, delay often intercepts life. The sweet hope of a longer life draws one to destruction, because while a man trusts that he can live longer in this world, he makes the time of penitence pass without penitence. But you, man, if you accept my counsel, will not defer penitence, because you are utterly ignorant what tomorrow will bring you. For he deserves to lose the time of penitence who has so often deserved to defer the zeal for repenting.

On the vanity of the present and on the eternal future.

The root of fear is raised in the mind of one who meditates, if the vanity of visible things and the invisible eternity are considered with studious attention. For all things that we discern in this world are wholly subject to vanity and corruption, and are to endure for only a very little time. All mortal things hang under uncertain chance and, by their own changeableness, promise flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow, or even now, while you are speaking, will cease to be yours. For we perceive nothing lasting and stable in this world, but see that all things change with time.

Now therefore ascend the watchtower of your mind, faithful monk, and consider how nothing are all the things that time contains, because Whatever visible thing is now seen will shortly decay. Take full consideration of things past, and see that what has passed away does not exist, and that what now seems to exist will, after a little while, no longer be.

Where are the kings of the nations, where the princes, where the leaders, where the rich, where those once powerful in the world? Where are all the lovers of the world, where the men who despised the steep path of heaven? Finally, where are all those once known to you in the world, whom death has meanwhile carried off while you have been in the cloister? Behold, from the beginning of the world, both those who lived for many years and those who lived for few have all died in their own generation; and according to the diversity of their merits, at the dictation of justice, they have also received different rewards.

The lovers of God, joined to the Creator of all, receive everlasting bright dwellings filled with inestimable joys; and the worshipers of the world, despising the commandments of God, once swollen here with honors, puffed up with knowledge, immersed in riches, given over to pleasures and vices, have gone down to hell to be tormented without end. What harm, I ask, does the once laborious contempt of the world, contrary to the flesh, now do to the saints in heaven, for which they now enjoy the glad vision of God forever? What profit now to the impious, buried in hell, is the consolation of the flesh once possessed, for which they now receive the torments of eternal damnation? Think on these things while it is profitable; meditate on these things while the opportunity for taking care is present.

Again, climbing higher, try with all your strength to fix the gaze of your mind in the abyss of infinite depth, and to consider how long that is which is eternal. Eternal is time that is enclosed by no end, bounded by no space. The saints of God will exult forever in blessed glory; sinners will burn forever in hell in misery. O eternity, name terrible without end: who will be able to think of you or speak of you without fear? Truly, he who thinks of you never sins eternally. Eternity has no end.

Hear a comparison, and though it will not be sufficient for eternity, receive fear from it. If a heap of sand were set up in the size of Mount Olympus, stretching to the sky, and from it after ten thousand years one little bird carried away only one grain, that mountain would by no means be said to last forever, but would be subject to an end; and although after innumerable years, nevertheless it would sometime cease to be. Yet all that time in which anything of the mountain remained, however very long it might be, would still seem as nothing in relation to eternity. For what is eternal receives no end even in imagination, nor does it admit hope of completion or limit.

Therefore the man is foolish, senseless, and mad who casts away this consideration of eternity, and uselessly spends the acceptable time granted him for deserving eternal goods. The hour will come, and is already hastening near, in which, no longer able to do better, he will learn what eternity is. But you, my monk, who desire to be faithful, cast from yourself every anxiety of the world; set all your care upon the love of God. Do nothing, say nothing, think nothing except what you know can lead you to the love of the Creator, or what pertains to the edification of others or to the pure necessity of the body.

Separate yourself, I pray, from low things, so that you may be able to delight in eternal goods. Let no anxiety of the flesh move you away from the inner tranquility of the mind; let no pleasure corrupt you. Strive to be always intent on prayers, as much as you can, with devotion, and again to lift yourself up more often through the affection of love.

On always having zeal for God.

The seventh root of the fear of God is called zeal, in which the monk is commanded to exercise himself no little. For no one who truly loves his lord tolerates calmly the injuries done to him. Therefore you, monk, who desire to be a faithful servant of Jesus Christ, do not neglect his zeal within yourself. Do not pretend not to see an injury to God when you see one, because whoever does not at once resist those who disparage his Lord is proved to love him too little. Let men know you as such a lover of God and enemy of vices that they do not dare to speak evil in your presence, nor to do any evil when they suspect you are watching.

Let them not presume against you. Be conspicuous for uprightness of soul, renowned for the merit of your life, worthy of reverence for your zeal. Let the upright love you as a servant of God; let the wicked dread your face as that of a judge. Let no one in your sight presume to do anything alien to good morals, since all should know that you cannot tolerate injury done to God.

Thus Phinehas the priest merited an everlasting covenant, when, by zealously defending the Lord’s law, he bravely appeased his anger. If you see order perishing in the monastery, if your brothers have begun in any way to corrupt regular observance, do not, if you are God’s servant, keep silence about their vices. Now set yourself bravely on behalf of the house of the Lord; exercise zeal for God as much as you can; destroy the counsels of the malicious; withstand the rashness of the proud. If you are a true lover of God, by your face alone you will scatter wicked gatherings. For no one will lay bare his plan before you if he suspects your zeal to be opposed to it. But if the wicked do not fear your presence when they are doing evil, they certainly recognize no zeal for God in you.

Therefore, to show yourself a true servant of Christ, you ought, for love of God, gladly to forgive injuries inflicted on yourself, and to pray to God for those who injure you. But injuries against the Lord, which it is not yours to forgive without his will, you should rather avenge out of zeal for righteousness. Let love of blood-kin cease in these matters; let the bond of friendship withdraw far away; zeal for God must rightly be preferred to all things. For friendship with a man must be maintained in such a way that it is never preferred to zeal for God.

Woe to monks and abbots who so boldly cast away the zeal of God, who place human familiarities before the divine command, who through foolish compassion conceal the vices of their subjects, who observe the traditions of the holy Rule neither in themselves nor in others. And what shall I say? We discern among cloistered monks that obedience to commands is despised, zeal for righteousness is scorned, observance of the Rule is contemned. Two or more contract among themselves a covenant of carnal friendship under the name of charity; the weak entrust the sicknesses of their souls to those weaker than themselves, though the friendship of God especially requires purity of mind.

Each one thinks his own companion better than the rest; one loves another, deceived not spiritually but carnally, because, since they do not raise their affections to God, they love nothing but the consolations of the flesh. But when you see a monk seeking friendship with a weak brother, you ought to judge him not a servant of God but a lover of the flesh. For he who truly occupies his heart in the love of God cares nothing for human friendship. The love of Jesus is enough for him in all things; outside it he seeks nothing further. But he who seeks the consolations of his mind in outward things shows by his deeds that he does not love God with his whole heart.

The love of God loves solitude, hates the tumult of men, and does not require the conversations of friends. O good Jesus, sweet is your love, because it pierces the heart of the one who loves you; seeing you, it desires to see you; having you, the soul longs to embrace you. Truly, he who loves you forgets himself; he meditates on nothing but the sweetest pleasure of you. There is nothing in the world that pleases one who loves you; nothing is found anywhere that the soul desires except for your sake.

O with how many sighs the mind wounded by love is distressed; with what abundant tears the face is drenched in secret, because as often as it thinks of the beloved’s face enthroned in heaven, so often it weeps that it is desolate on earth. Meanwhile the mind, languishing with love, often attempts to say something about its most beloved Jesus; it tries also to rouse others to his love. But as soon as it begins to utter the sweetest name of Jesus, unwillingly, from the greatness of love, it falls silent. For the love of Jesus is expressed by no words, but is felt with sweetness in the secret of the mind.

I know who said, “My love is crucified.” Who is your love, O servant of God? Why do you weep? Why do you groan? Ignatius: “My love is crucified, and shall I not mourn? My Lord is dead, and shall I be able to hold back my tears?” Do not weep, O faithful soul, for although your love died to redeem you from death, yet now he has risen from the dead to crown you in heaven. Be faithful unto death, and he will give you the crown of life.

On the mode and degrees of divine love: a collected conclusion of this second region.

Since no one suddenly becomes perfect, nor can anyone by his own strength suddenly ascend to that supreme summit of divine love, I now think it useful briefly to note certain modes or degrees of loving God. Therefore, for moving the human heart to divine love, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is, in my judgment, more effective than all other things, if it is considered in a person’s mind purely, sweetly, fervently, perseveringly, and diligently. For truly, whoever often recalls to memory the life, Passion, and death of our Savior, with compassion and thanksgiving, according to their chief and principal articles, prepares a swift ascent of the heart to divine love. But we shall deal fittingly with this most holy occupation of the mind concerning the Lord’s Passion in the second principal part of this work, where we shall set out more fully the manner of spiritual exercise. As far as the meaning of what has been said in this place is concerned, I find three modes of loving God, which I shall briefly explain in order.

The first mode commands that you love sweetly him who loves you, and that you join your whole self to him sweetly, so that your heart loves nothing outside God and seeks nothing from elsewhere. For since God is the whole good, he alone desires to possess the whole heart of the one who loves him; he drives it far from displeasing thoughts. Therefore, if you wish to love sweetly, love totally. For either the whole of divine love perfects, or nothing does. Let meditation on the Passion of Jesus Christ our Savior possess you wholly, until love grows sweetly strong in you. You must despise everything that flatters in the flesh, if you desire to come to the love of God. For no one can sweetly love God in this life so long as he is convicted of loving anything in the world. Indeed, love of the world is utterly contrary to divine love, because where one is admitted to the inner chambers of the heart, the other is forbidden to be present.

But how much sweetness, how much delight, how much joy of mind the love of God produces in the heart of the lover, no one fully understands except one who, having despised all the things and events of the world, has loved God alone for a long time. The heart of one who loves God loves nothing that is in the world; it despises riches, honors, and the favor of the age; it does not fear to undergo any adversities for the love of its Lord. The love of God is never idle; it always desires to come to its own source; it refuses no labors to be endured in this world. Therefore let him who does not wish to become slothful love.

One’s neighbor also must be loved sweetly for God’s sake, and must in no way be offended against God or justice. Each person should always show himself to his brother, in words and deeds, such as he expects others to be toward himself. For he truly loves his neighbor who exposes his goods, his body, and his soul for him. This Christ taught; this the Son of God did for us. Indeed, whoever says that he truly believes in Christ ought himself to walk just as Christ walked. He does not truly love Christ who does not keep his commandments. For he says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you.” We are members of one head, Jesus Christ; and then we believe in him when we observe his commandment concerning love toward God and toward neighbor. Therefore let us love our neighbor, because he is a member in Christ together with us, so that just as one member in the body suffers with another, so a brother may humbly be helped by a brother for the love of Christ.

The second mode commands you to love wisely, and to seek nothing in divine love except God. Stretch out your affection toward that Word which was in the beginning with God; lift up your mind above everything that is created, because unless you leave behind yourself and all things that are in the world, you will not be able to come to him whom you love. Finally, if you desire to love God wisely, do not think yourself to be anything else; for where a person thinks himself to be something, he already loves foolishly.

The third mode commands that you love strongly, and that you never fear to expose body and soul for the love of God. He is not a strong lover of God who is afraid to undergo death for him. For love is strong as death. One’s neighbor is loved wisely if it is not the person but the vice that is hated. But he is loved strongly if every injury is forgiven from the heart, by doing good, on the same day.

The second region ends.

Preface to the third treatise of the first part, which describes the supreme region of the spirit of cloistered persons.

At last, with the Lord’s help, as I am about to write of that supreme region of the spirit, I am shaken by fear and shame together: for, small as I am, I fear to speak of the greatest things, and I greatly blush to teach what I have not sufficiently experienced. For what mind of any man, however much exercised, could recognize the state of a mind resting sweetly in God? Or what [unclear], even of the most eloquent orator, could explain the sweetness of inward contemplation? Indeed, the exercise of this third region surpasses human understanding for the greater part. In it the mind of a purified man, through the fervor of divine love, is carried above itself and, while its natural essence remains, is lulled and absorbed with wonderful sweetness in the abyss of divine contemplation. It is oppressed by so great a sweetness of inward majesty that it seems able neither to understand nor to express its own state. Once the operation of sense has plainly been left behind, it wholly surpasses even the intellect; and, as though leaving itself still further, without imagination, reasoning, or understanding, it is raised by affection above itself to that supreme summit of divine darkness.

But when it has utterly failed away from itself, it does not act but rests; nor, when returned to itself, can it understand what it has undergone, or reveal to anyone the manner of its elevation. For this elevation of the mind into God is so pure and so sublime that not only can one who has not experienced it not understand it, but even one who has experienced it cannot fully explain in words what it is like. But what shall I be able to say about the mountain of divine darkness, which I have not yet deserved to penetrate? For the well of inward contemplation is deep, and I am weak: I have brought neither a bucket fit for these waters, nor have I prepared steps suitable for climbing to the heights. Polished words do not befit a fool; nor ought an inexperienced and cold man to speak of the secrets of divine contemplation, when he still stands with the weak in the valleys. For only he speaks fruitfully of profound matters who is illumined by the ray of the twofold spirit.

Yet since I am a man placed under obedience to the annual chapter, I am compelled to accept the command of that synod and, according to my strength, to complete the work set before me. Therefore I enter the third region of cloistered persons under the guidance of the venerable father, lord Johannes of Bursfelde, a devout abbot, so that what he described in learned and truthful speech, I may seem to reduce, as far as I can, to my own manner of speaking, in obedience to the chapter.

Here begins the third region of the soul, which is called spiritual, in which the highest tranquility of the mind is found.

The third, or supreme, region of the soul is called spiritual; in it the highest rest and tranquility of the mind abide. And this region is compared to the empyrean heaven, in which there is the true rest of all and the true happiness of souls. The spirit dwelling in this region leaves behind what is beneath reason and, raised by love into God, ascends wondrously. For whatever it does in this most holy region is judged wholly divine. Here the human spirit, rapt above itself, receives the divine inpouring and, lulled in the darkness of divine contemplation, withdrawn from all creatures, sweetly rests. In this region almighty God directs the spirit of the one contemplating him; he perfects the simplified intellectual powers of the soul, recalled from every phantasm into the inner chamber, according to the objects of their own tendencies; and he leads the mind, stripped of every multiplicity, to himself, the one principle, making it one with himself, not by nature, but by gracious participation. The inhabitants of this supreme region are truly spiritual men, who, having despised all the things and affections of the world, love nothing in this world except God, desire nothing inordinately, but through inward affection absorbed by [unclear].

by the divine Spirit, thirsts intensely for God himself; he burns with an unceasing desire for love of him. For they are driven in God by so great a fervor of love that he raises them above themselves; they generally leave behind all intellectual operations, and, carried into the abyss of divine contemplation, admit nothing at all except God. There, existing insensibly through the grace of love, they become one with God, while the property of their natures remains intact, by the gift of participation. For the holy apostle of Jesus Christ says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit.” And again he says: “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God.” The same apostle also shows himself to be a citizen of this most holy region when he cries out to the Philippians: “Our conversation is in heaven.”

For as long as we are in the body we are exiled from the Lord; but as though through sleep we are sweetly led to our homeland when in mind and spirit we have our conversation in heavenly things. I say “through sleep” not properly, but by a remote comparison. For in sleep we go forth among images of things intelligible to us, the forms being preserved in the imagination; but in contemplation, beyond every imagination, we are raised by pure mind and spirit to God. And therefore this supreme region of the soul is called spiritual, from which all religious receive the name of spirituality.

Woe to us. We are called spiritual from this most blessed region; we are named religious, lovers of God; and yet we never climb the summit of this mountain by the height of contemplation, but, weak with the weak, always lie sick upon the bed of carnal desires. Why do we bear a holy name, who are not holy? Let us strive, then, with all our strength, through the continual exercise of the middle region, to ascend to the height of this supreme summit, if we truly desire to obtain the name of a spiritual way of life. In this region charity holds command, wisdom the consulship; in it nothing is loved except God, nothing disorderly is committed.

This most holy region belongs to the empyrean heaven, because those whom it spiritually receives as citizens it sends straight to the joys of heaven. For just as the lowest region of the flesh sends its dying clients to hell, and the middle region of reason sends its own to purgatory, so this region sends its perfect worshipers, when they depart, to heaven. The dignity of this third and supreme region is expressed by many prerogatives and is especially commended in seven articles, as will be said in order.

That this supreme region of the spirit of the cloistered is shown by a pleasing comparison.

First, then, this third region of the soul is described by a pleasing comparison, because it is compared to the highest, empyrean heaven. For just as all things are tranquil in the empyrean heaven, so on this summit of the supreme region the mind of the person contemplating God is disturbed by no agitations. Here is the highest rest of the contemplating soul; here no crowd of vices dwells; no bitterness of mind approaches at all. In the empyrean heaven, indeed, the majesty of God is seen by the holy spirits with an ineffable gift; here, in darkness, through the desire of love, he is seen above understanding. There God is all things in all; here nothing among all things is pleasing except God. There it is granted to the saints to rest endlessly from their labors; here the mind is permitted, in resting, to taste beforehand the unspeakable sweetness of inward delight.

There is no greater happiness in heaven, and there is not in the world so sweet a tranquility as in this region. Blessed indeed are those who have merited to ascend this mountain of divine contemplation, who love nothing at all in this world and always desire nothing other than to cleave to God. How secure is the conscience of these citizens, how joyful their conversation, where no evil is committed and nothing is desired except that supreme, unchangeable good. For the mind purified by divine love, which has truly and perseveringly ascended this region, desires nothing carnal, nothing disorderly, but, wholly raised by desire into contemplation of the highest majesty, rests sweetly in God alone. O who can [unclear] the inward sweetness could truly express the lover of God: where the mind recalls the powers and capacities of the soul from the dispersion of multiplicity into one, and, fired by burning affections, lifts them into the chamber of the spirit; and directs its gaze by love toward that supreme, unchangeable Good, utterly rejecting from itself every created and creatable multitude; the spirit gathers itself into one, so that, united within itself, it may seek to rise without the impediment of multiplicity to its own principle, by which it is one. To the one principle of all things, clearly, unity alone can attain, because unity flees multiplicity and seeks the one. For the more you yield to multiplicity, the more you withdraw from unity. Therefore the mind, in this supreme region of the spirit in which man dwells, when it seeks to ascend by contemplation to its principle through love, is accustomed to cast away from itself every multiplicity clinging to imagination or understanding, so that, gathered in its own unity, it may be able to direct itself ardently toward that one with the simple affection of love, whom it knows to be above every position.

That this supreme region of the spirit is sweet and lovable by reason of its nearness.

Article two.

Secondly, this supreme region of the spirit is sweet and most pleasant by likeness and singular nearness. For the citizen of this most holy region is separated from the citizens above by only one clay wall, so to speak, since as long as the spirit inhabits the flesh, it cries out to heaven as though through a wall. But the clay wall of flesh is the prison from which the spirit, when set free and about to migrate to heaven, goes forth when it is separated from the body by death. But the spirit wounded by sins, which cannot lift itself to this region through the pure affection of love, is still said to stand farther away from the empyrean heaven. Those, however, who dwell in this most quiet region are nearest to the empyrean heaven, because, weighed down by no stains of sins, they despise all earthly and carnal things, and always long to live in mind and spirit among heavenly things.

Indeed, those who inhabit the empyrean heaven and those who dwell in the third region have one and the same delight. But this is the difference: these contemplate God in a mirror and enigma, while those contemplate him in clear vision. The sweetness of those contemplating is on both sides; here it is great, there it is greatest; here it is in the fierce desire of love, there in possession of the most blessed vision.

In this supreme region of divine contemplation the rational spirit recalls its powers and capacities into its own chamber; and there, free from every phantasm, it is empty of them, raises itself above itself into the dense darkness of the divine, and, lulled to sleep by ecstatic love, rests sweetly. Here no troublesome confusion of thoughts moves about, no imagining of phantasms, but the bare mind is lifted upward and contemplates without any thought or any imagination. For whenever the mind itself opens access to thoughts, it shows that it is descending again to the middle region, which belongs to reason. But since the mind of man cannot always remain unmoved on the summit of divine contemplation, it must often return to the rational exercise of the second region. If, however, it has slipped down into sensual passions, then it has again descended to the lowest region. But the spirit of the true lover of God, although because of the frailty of the flesh it cannot always remain in the pleasantness of contemplation, nevertheless strives more often, through the affections of fire, to lift itself to that region, so that it may fulfill the exercise of reason in such a way that it does not entirely lose the sweetness of inward delight. O how good it is to cling to the Lord; how sweet it is to attend to God alone, so that the mind may thirst for him above all things and always long to embrace him with burning desires. Indeed, the one who stands in this region is nearest to the empyrean heaven, and therefore is inflamed toward it with the greatest desires of love. O how many groans and tears the mind fervent with love is accustomed to send forth; how ardently it sighs for heavenly things, since the nearer it is to the empyrean heaven through the secret of contemplation while standing in this supreme region, the more ardent its desire to go forth from the prison of the body is known to be. Thus

The third article: this supreme region of the soul is called divine instruction.

This supreme region of the soul is called divine instruction, in which the mind, burning with divine love, is taught not by man but by the Holy Spirit. For Christ said to his lovers in the holy Gospel: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” And again, that word of the prophet: “And they shall all be taught by God.” The Holy Spirit of eternity dwells in the heart of the one who loves [unclear], and illumines it by his invisible teaching.

In this region the spirit chooses true wisdom, the best part of Mary, in silent tranquillity; mystical theology is taught in secret, in the ineffable sweetness of the divine darkness; the mind, disposed toward its beloved by the fervor of most holy love, speaks in secret with him and continually raises itself to him through desire. This wisdom, or mystical theology, can indeed be commended by man, but it cannot be taught except in divine instruction. For it is the work of the Holy Spirit when the mind is illumined in true contemplation.

But we must consider that mystical theology is acquired through the exercise of a purified affection and is taught through the fire of love. Speculative theology, which we call scholastic, is learned through the exercise of the intellect, while the mind devotes itself continually to study. For the acquisition of mystical theology, the purification of the affection from every entanglement is required, so that the will, depraved through aversion, may be reformed toward its beginning through the quest of inward love. For unless the affection has been purified from every disordered concupiscence, it does not ascend to the height of this most sacred wisdom. But if it has cast off sensual passions, if the human will has been conformed to the divine will, the mind is raised upward through fiery love and is lifted by anagogical movements into the immensity of the divine darkness.

No one understands the certainty of this theology unless he receives it; no one receives it unless he seeks it alone above all things through the sighs of love. The psalmist sought this when he prayed to the Lord: “O that my ways may be directed to keep your statutes at all times.” For by such movements of desire the holy man was borne upward to obedience to the divine will, so that in that same Psalm 118 he said almost no verse in which he did not place some word equivalent to the divine judgments. The exercise of this purification is begun in the second region and is completed in this one. For no small labor is undertaken, that the affection may be purified from the concupiscences of the world. But once the exercise of spiritual reformation has been taken up, the mind gradually advances in love, desires to ascend to this region by sure steps, hastens through desire to the invisible school of this theology, and, sighing with continual groans, knocks at the door of divine compassion.

But the mind is not admitted into the secret of this mystical wisdom unless, after complete purification of the affection, it is freed from every creature and unites itself to itself, and withdraws far from every reason or imagination of thinkable things. For unless it withdraws from every creature, it does not approach the Creator, who is above all things. Therefore in this school of divine instruction the Holy Spirit is believed to preside over those who learn: he teaches a person to love nothing in this world and to conform himself in all things to the will of God. Happy is he who has deserved to be the disciple of this master; happy is he who has entered this school through the desire of love, for in mystical silence he receives wonderful things that God has hidden from those who do not love him.

That this supreme region of the spirit is founded in simplicity.

Fourth, this most holy region of the spirit is called founded in simplicity, in which the mind, not through essence [unclear].

but through the love of adhesion it is united to its immutable one principle. For, as we have said above, that highest good, God, is one; and our soul cannot draw near to it unless, stripped of all multiplicity, which it receives by attraction, imagination, and understanding, it strives to present itself wholly one to itself. For the soul naturally desires to reach the highest good; but the more it is divided in its operation through multiplicity, the less fit it is found to come to it. For multiplicity is opposed to unity, and the more the mind turns itself toward many things, the more it withdraws from unity. One, two, three, four are ten. You withdraw from the one when you are multiplied in number. Return to the one if you desire to have the beginning. For the one is the beginning of all things; if you add anything to it in your mind, you at once withdraw from it. When you say “one,” you say “beginning.” If you say “two,” you have already abandoned the beginning. Therefore, so that you may always be able to contemplate your beginning, take care at every time, stripped of all multiplicity, to make yourself one.

For since all good things are from the first good, and every love, toward whatever good it is borne, is naturally kindled by that same good, our love cannot be touched by any goods or rest in any final end unless, naked and pure, it strives at last to return to its own beginning. For union comes about only by the power of the one itself; and for no other reason do we more readily say that things more alike are united with one another than because we see that they are one in quality. Therefore the soul is believed to be able to be united with the one highest principle of things only when, stripped of all multiplicity and united even to itself, it is lifted up to God by most fervent love. Just as there is no union between things different in quality, so between God and a soul divided in itself there can be no adhesion.
