Let all worldly anxieties depart far from here; let all thoughts withdraw. Let nothing be thought here except what belongs to the consummation of so great a mystery; let nothing be turned over in the mind except what befits the presence of so great a majesty and glory. For here no office of human strength is performed, but the miracle of divine majesty is enacted: the Son of God is offered to the Father; the body of our Redeemer is truly received; the mystery of our reconciliation is celebrated. Therefore, standing at the altar, let the priest remember that he stands before invisible majesty, and let him beware of thinking of anything else.

After celebration, careful custody of the mind is to be kept.

After the celebration, or after communion of the Lord’s body and blood, let the devout monk offer thanksgiving to almighty God, and throughout the whole day let him keep himself, by spiritual exercise, in the purity and devotion of mind he has conceived. Let him direct his affections to God with fiery rays, and not grow lukewarm from his holy purpose. Above all, let him strive to love nothing in this world, but to raise his heart continually, stripped completely of all earthly affections, toward the fire of divine love. Let him always consider how from now on he may order his life as though anew, in the holy fervor of his way of life, and let him humbly dispose himself for the more frequently repeated reception of so great a Guest. Then, during the day, in the labors enjoined on him, let him quite often offer some prayer to God the Father in the power and union of that sacrament, so that through the exercise of holy communion and regular obedience he may kindle himself more fully in divine love. And we attain this divine love especially through the power of this venerable sacrament, if, in memory of the Lord’s passion, we are renewed by the grace of union through communicating in it more often. For truly the devout mind of a person is kindled, through communion of this most sacred sacrament, into the fervor of divine love by its effective working; and, having utterly denied itself, it is transformed, united by grace into Christ. Therefore the more each person, denied to himself through true resignation, has offered himself to the Lord as a living sacrifice in memory of the Lord’s passion, the more disposed he will be to celebrate worthily.

After private Masses. Returning to the cell.

When the celebration of Masses has been finished, and the thanksgivings have been completed according to custom, let the monk return to his cell; and, after first saying the customary prayer as above at Matins, let him recollect himself for a little while, and kindle himself more fully from his holy purpose toward perseverance. Then, turned toward the Lord, let him say: Prayer.

I beseech you, sweetest Lord Jesus, through the power of your most holy body and blood which I have received, though unworthy: grant me the sweetness of your love, sincerity of brotherly affection, strength in temptation, purity in heart, and discipline in conduct, so that, by your bounty, I may satisfy my profession, and make vigorous progress in your most holy love. Then, until the first signal for choir, let him read something good, meditate, or pray, or certainly write, and let him fervently apply himself to the work enjoined on him by obedience.

At the first signal before choir, before High Mass.

When the first signal has sounded for the hour which, according to custom, precedes High Mass, let the monk at once put aside everything he has in his hands and read the preparatory prayers for choir, just as they are set out above before Matins. Afterward let him go to choir with reverence and maturity, bowing and praying according to the rite set down above.

At High Mass.

At the ringing for High Mass you may read the proper hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward, as time permits, recall to mind something from the preface set before the private Masses. For the sum of our salvation is placed in the merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, nor is any good work of ours believed meritorious unless it is offered in his power. The memory of this passion is carried out in the celebration of Masses, where the innocent Lamb, slain for us, is offered to God the Father in an ineffable mystery. Therefore from our Savior alone, the Lord Christ, whom we believe to have suffered for us, do we truly hope for salvation. And so whatever the Church asks in the collects, she humbly asks God the Father that it be given to her through him. This regard Let our devout cenobite keep in his heart the merit of the Lord’s passion, upon which the whole office of the Mass may sweetly return, as upon a foundation stone. For every Mass, of whatever kind it may be, which is said in the holy Church of God, is at all times referred to the merit of the Lord’s passion.

On the Introit of the Mass.

We do not intend to explain the office of the Mass point by point, since each of us can find many expositions by others; rather, we wish to give the devout brothers an occasion for meditation, whom we know to be inflamed with inward desires. You may, however, in meditation refer the first part of the introit and the verse to the incarnation of the Lord, and refer the repetition with the Gloria to his nativity. Nevertheless, you must diligently consider what the introit contains according to the literal sense, so that you may be able to find a spiritual understanding suitable for yourself. For nothing is done in vain in the divine office; rather, all things are filled with mysteries and sacred actions.

On the Kyrie eleison.

Kyrie eleison is Greek, composed of a noun and a verb, and among them they are two words. The first is from kyrios, which means “Lord”; kyrie is said in the vocative. The second is from eleeo, which means “I have mercy”; eleeson, “have mercy,” is pronounced in the imperative. From this comes Kyrie eleison, that is, “Lord, have mercy,” by elision for Kyrie eleison, since a vowel before a vowel can be elided for a better sound.

Three times, therefore, he says Kyrie eleison to the Father, so that he who, out of exceeding charity, willed his Son to be incarnate of the Virgin and to die for us, may also be willing to come to our aid by his mercy in our necessities.

To the Son also we say Christe eleison three times, in which we pray him to come to our aid.

Three times also we utter Kyrie eleison to the Holy Spirit, in which we humbly call upon him for our help, according to his ineffable goodness.

On the Gloria in excelsis.

Then Gloria in excelsis Deo is said in the singular number, in which we confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit to be one sole true God in a Trinity of persons and a unity of substance.

Accordingly, during that angelic hymn the cenobite ought to be very devout, and, so to speak, especially attentive to each word; in it the gift of peace is promised to men of good will, and God is humbly adored by us in various expressions.

At the Collects.

When the collects or prayers are offered by the priest to God, the devout cenobite should think of nothing else, but, listening to the priest’s words, should present his own desire to God in agreement with them.

At the Epistle.

When the epistle is read, you must attend diligently to everything, and give spiritual thanks to God with the greatest fervor, because, leaving behind the Jewish people, he so mercifully willed to call you and your forebears from Gentile error to his faith.

At the Gradual.

At the gradual, alleluia, sequence, and tract, think how long a desire the holy fathers had, who before the incarnation of Christ longed for his coming. Then consider with how many labors and injuries your Savior was wearied for you in this world for thirty-three years, who voluntarily gave himself up to death for your salvation. Then call to mind the long exile of your soul in the flesh and amid dangers, so that by this abundant meditation, full of misery, you may inflame your affection toward divine love.

During the Gospel.

At the holy Gospel, with your mind lifted up to the Lord, give thanks with rejoicing, because the merciful Father willed you to be born of Christian parents, and because he made you a sharer in his holy and most sweet teaching.

During the Creed.

When the symbol of the catholic faith is sung, consider all its words and mysteries with humble fervor of spirit, [unclear].

hasten at once to recollect yourself within yourself, so that you may be able to give thanks worthily to him who called you to the faith without any merit of your own, and to raise yourself up in the inward love of the spirit. Consider, if you can, or rather as much as you can, how great, exalted, and immeasurable is the Son of God, who for your sake willed to become incarnate; how hard and bitter were the things he endured for you.

At the Offertory.

When the offertory is taking place, apply your mind, together with the host to be consecrated, to the offering, and ponder what is being done there mystically. For the host is round and white. In its whiteness are set forth the purity, innocence, and suffering humanity of our Savior, to be offered to God the Father for us against all our impurities; in its roundness his immeasurable divinity is offered to us as the appointed reward. Say therefore to the Lord: Prayer.

I have no worthy gift to offer you, almighty God; I hand myself over to you as a sacrifice. Receive, therefore, holy Father, in union with the most holy offering of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, me as an eternal gift to you and as a perpetual servant; and give me the continual fire of your holy love, that I may always be able to render you pleasing service. Through the same.

Prayer.

I offer you, almighty God, the life, passion, and death of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, for my sins, for the holy Roman and universal Church, for the supreme pontiff, for our bishop, for our abbot, for all my brothers, for the union of our observance, for our whole order wherever it may be, for the salvation of all the faithful, for the conversion of unbelievers, and for the redemption of the souls of the faithful existing in the pains of purgatory. Receive, I beseech you, holy Father, this offering of mine in union with that charity with which you received the same our Lord Jesus Christ dying for us on the cross, and may it be pleasing to you.

During the Preface.

When the preface is being said, take care to raise your mind from all earthly things to heavenly things, and to prepare it to praise the Lord with the holy angels. Remember that through the merit of his holy passion you have been called to the fellowship of the angels, and take care that through observance of the commandments you may come to it.

At the Sanctus.

With your mind lifted upward, glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord, to whom the Sanctus is sung, and humbly adore his majesty with the holy angels at all times.

During the Canon.

After the Sanctus, during the canon, you may take up meditation on the Lord’s passion, and offer it, article by article, especially the greater and principal ones, to God the Father for yourself, or for others, or for any necessity. Say, therefore, in this or a similar manner: O holy Father, I offer you the bloody sweat and tears of our Lord Jesus Christ, your most beloved Son, in that charity and union in which he voluntarily offered himself to you in death for us: for my sins, or for that brother, or for that servant-girl, or for that necessity. And I ask you, through the pain of the wounds of that same sweetest Son of yours, and through the pouring out of his most holy blood and the power of his most innocent death: have mercy on me, or on that person, or grant us this or that, and so forth. Through the same our Lord.

With the other articles of the Lord’s passion you will be able to proceed in the same way, and to enlarge upon them in offering according to the intention of your affection.

At the Elevation.

If, at the elevation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your mind is not occupied with higher things, you may pray to the Lord, who is truly present, in this way: You are the King of glory, O Christ. You are the everlasting Son of the Father. You, to deliver man, did not shrink from the Virgin’s womb, and so on to the end. For this part of the hymn, Saint Thomas Aquinas is read to have prayed to the Lord during the elevation.

At the Agnus Dei.

When the Agnus Dei is sung, lift up your mind to the Lord Jesus with singular trust, and humbly pray that he may receive you into perpetual peace. To him, for whose love all things...

whom you have left. Direct your affection toward him; after receiving holy communion, ask that it may be made steadfast by him, by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

At the “Ite, missa est.”

When at the end the “Ite, missa est” is sung, cause your mind to be lifted up with the holy angels returning into heaven, so that, while Jesus presides in majesty, you may deserve to behold by desire him whom, in the sacrament of the Mass now offered to the Father, you can no longer see on earth. Therefore kindle your desire by the image of desolation, in the manner of those who are unwillingly separated from their own friends.

Say, then, in your heart: Meditation.

Behold, my Lord has returned to heaven; he has left me desolate on earth. What am I doing here among mortals, when I have one who is immortal? Why do I not follow him? Woe to me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of darkness; my soul has long been a sojourner. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but who will deliver me, unhappy man that I am, from the body of this death? O most loving Lord Jesus, my hope, O God and Savior of my soul, draw me after you; I will run in the fragrance of your ointments. O my sweet love, do not forget me to the end, but deign frequently to lift up my mind to you, so that, since I cannot see you bodily while set in this mortality, at least, lifted up in affection and desire in your most holy love, I may deserve more often to behold you in spirit in glory. O my salvation, O heart of my heart, most loving Jesus, do not abandon me or despise me; be a gracious helper to me, and direct me always in your most holy will, so that I may truly be able to please you.

After High Mass and the following hour.

After the end of the hour that immediately follows High Mass, return to your cell with the customary reverence described above; pour out prayers to the Lord with fervor of spirit, as we taught after Matins. Spend the remaining time in meditations. Consider the foulness of sin, how it separates from God and eternally condemns the one who is turned away and does not repent. Take care, therefore, to turn your will wholly to God with the firmest resolution, and to avoid the contagion of sin at all times with all your strength.

On the regular meal.

When the signal is rung for the meal, have compassion from the heart for the sick, the needy, and the poor who suffer want; and when you can do nothing else, pray for them to the Lord. Consider that among Christians there are many far better than you whom harsh poverty oppresses in this life, to whom not even coarse bread necessary for food is offered, nor even the thinnest clothing supplied for covering the body. But you, though you are a monk and a despiser of the world, are clothed in the best garments and sit at table like a prince; brothers better than you set food before you to satiety; in short, all necessities are supplied to you, an unworthy sinner, to the point of nausea by the servants of God. Consider, then, what end this abundance of things will have in a monk: for on entering religion you professed poverty, yet now in religion you feast more splendidly than the rich of the world. Take care, therefore, that you not live ungrateful for such great benefits of God, but according to the rule you have professed. Pray for those who contribute temporal substance to your monastery, that almighty God may mercifully grant them eternal life.

On reading at table.

When you are sitting at table, be composed while eating. Do not look this way and that, but endeavor to eat humbly and with thanksgiving the food set before you, as much as is fitting for the necessity of nature. Carefully consider what is read at table, so that, just as the body is refreshed with its food, so the soul may not be deprived of its own refreshment. Accustom your mind while eating to rise frequently to heavenly things, and through the word The nourishment of holy reading is never lacking to us as we eat, and it sweetly inflames us with divine compunction. For the true and inward worshiper of God, whenever even amid meals he hears something read about the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, the fervor of divine love, or the kingdom of the heavenly homeland, at once groans with an immense desire, is kindled in the ardor of love, and, compelled by exceeding sweetness, weeps. For indeed the mind that truly loves the Lord Jesus, as soon as it hears his name or beholds the image of the crucified, is dissolved in compunction and is lifted up in affection to his feet or to his embrace.

For thanksgiving.

When the meal is finished, give thanks to the Lord; and while you go to the church under the psalm, direct your mind upward and intercede for benefactors, living and dead. If after thanksgiving you add some special prayer for the dead, you do well.

On the regular reading.

Leaving the refectory for the cell, if it is not a fast day, complete the customary prayer; then read something good for edification, meditate, or do or write the work that has been assigned to you. But if it is a fast day, take up the volume of your study and enter the place of regular reading; sitting with the others, read in silence what you wish. But if you are asked by the president to say something good, answer humbly with a few useful words, without curious citations. Do not use a very long speech, nor bring forward the vain curiosities of secular people among them; do not entangle your brothers sitting around you in crooked or distorted words, but express the thought of your mind simply in few words, unless perhaps the president, for a definite reason, orders you to make a longer speech.

The monk’s exercises after dinner until vespers.

Consideration VI.

After the reading, return to your cell. You should always [unclear] some prayer before your works, and in everything you do ask for the help of God. When you are in your cell, do not be idle, but do something good, especially what the abbot has enjoined by obedience. Now pray, now write, read something good or meditate; for the cell makes an idle monk either a beast or a demon. But we shall speak of these things in their proper place below. Take care to spend your time usefully, for in a short while you will have to render account of all of it to God.

On dwelling in the cell and the works to be done there.

There are three places in which a devout monk who loves God ought often to be found: namely, church, cell, and, at its proper time, refectory. But he should not permit himself to wander about the monastery, for it is written of the wicked, the reprobate, and the wandering monks: “The wicked walk in a circle.” But of the just man Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of God from his youth; he will sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself.” The works proper to the cell are these: first, to attend to commands; second, to read what is useful; third, to apply oneself to suitable meditation; fourth, to pray frequently; fifth, to rest fittingly. We shall speak of these briefly in order.

In the cell, first you must attend to commands.

First, when you are in the dwelling of your cell, learn to attend to commands, and do not prefer your idle devotions to obedience. For Scripture says: “Obedience is better than foolish offerings and victims, and to listen is better than to offer sacrifice.” Therefore, if something has been assigned to you to work at in the cell, do not transgress the paths of obedience on any pretext, but strive diligently to perform the work imposed on you for love of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the merit of holy obedience. Hence Hugh, lover of quiet, says: Gladly remain in the cell, and always do something in it that may edify you; and when something is enjoined by a superior, reckon that it is not your right [unclear].

You also have on this point the prohibition of our most holy father Benedict in the Rule, which forbids you to go out and range about without permission.

Secondly, in the cell you must read profitably.

It especially befits a monk, while he is in the cell, always to read something good and to occupy himself profitably in all things. For sacred reading overcomes the temptations of the devil, calms the fires of the flesh, makes one despise the world, and raises the mind to heavenly things. For Jerome, lover of divine Scripture, truly said: “Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” Not all things are to be read by all monks; one who is still weak in spirit must be instructed only in simple teachings. And Hugh says to the monk who loves simplicity: Do not read in order to be considered a teacher, nor read curiosities that do not edify, for vain reading generates vain thoughts and extinguishes devotion of mind. Therefore simple things, not lofty things, devout things, not curious things, are to be read by the simpler monks, so that those who, because of slowness of understanding, are not learned in higher matters may not become dissipated in vain ones. But we do not forbid suitable studies to those who are stronger in judgment, for all things are clean to the clean, and nothing that is read harms the truly devout. Nevertheless let no one claim for himself a strength of spirit that he does not have, but let him place the matter in the discretion of the abbot, who may judge whether he is fit for freedom in reading.

Thirdly, in the cell you must attend at proper times to meditations.

As a flower springs from the root, so meditation is generated from reading. If the reading has been vain, the meditation too will be fruitless and useless. For the fruit of reading is meditation, and the offspring of meditation is prayer. Therefore you must attend at proper times to holy meditations, so that you may also learn sometimes to raise your mind in contemplation through the fervor of divine love. For meditation itself lifts up the mind and commits the study of reading to memory.

Fourthly, in the cell you must attend to frequent prayer.

The holy Apostle teaches us to devote ourselves to prayer without ceasing, for just as breath is always necessary to us for the life of the flesh, so continuous prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind. For as we are instructed for good by readings, so by prayers we are freed from evil. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. For prayer refreshes the wearied mind, extinguishes the fire of carnal desire, forms one’s character, and drives away demons. If you wish always to be with God, always pray. But if your prayer is pure, simple, and bare, poured out to God through fervor of love, it cannot fail to be fruitful.

Fifthly, in the cell you must rest fittingly.

He rests badly who commits many evils. He rests well who despises all the occupations of the world. Be quiet in the cell, so that you may not wander here and there with any thought, but remain pure and tranquil with your whole mind, so that you may deserve to obtain savory knowledge. For the saint says in his poem: Wisdom instructs a tranquil mind, free from cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast. And again he says: Those who are at rest can search the law, if hearts free from noise are empty and unencumbered. Therefore, so that the mind intent on holy studies may be helped, let divine love conquer carnal quarrels. Remain quiet, then, in the cell, and you will be able to know the truth by loving it. For the mind will not be able to be tranquil and capable of divine wisdom when the body is restless. Hence Hugh says: In the dormitory be quiet, lest another be disturbed because of you. But when you wake, or when you desire to sleep, let the memory of God’s goodness always come to you with thanksgiving, because he himself always watches over us, so that he may guard from every evil us who humbly serve him. When you go to your bed, first [unclear].

On thinking or meditating about God you should allow yourself to fall asleep, so that you may sweetly be lulled to rest amid holy thoughts. For as your occupations have been while awake, so also will be your repose while asleep, and such also will your dreams be. For a mind burning with the single love of God, neither sleeping nor waking, will be able to forget its beloved, as the bride says in the Canticle: “I sleep, and my heart watches.”

At Vespers. Seventh consideration.

When the first bell for Vespers has been heard, and after the customary prayer, “Blessed be the name of the Lord,” has been said, while the others are permitted to busy themselves with secular affairs, give thanks to the almighty Lord, who has willed you to be free from them in order to serve him. Then gather yourself back within, or you may meditate on something concerning the Lord’s Passion, until the second bell sounds and you go to choir. For in my judgment there is no better meditation for beginners and for those making progress, toward compunction and devotion of mind, than that which takes its beginning from devout affections concerning the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ.

At the Vigils of the Dead.

When the vigil has been reckoned after Vespers, you may recite the hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward think somewhat on the immense charity of God with which he loves faithful souls. Then, as much as you can, consider in how great desolation those holy souls are placed in purgatory, since it is a great pain for a spirit separated from the body and longing to return to the center of its own beginning: not to be able yet to behold the face of its Creator with full enjoyment, but to be forced to wait in pains and torments most grievous to itself. For so great is the desolation, sadness, and grief of a soul separated, placed in pains, and longing to come to God, that no kind of torments known to us in this world could be compared with its sorrow. For there is no comparison of bodily sadness and desolation with the state of a separated spirit, established in the delay of its return to its own beginning.

Therefore, as much as you can, have compassion on the desolation of the faithful souls groaning in the prison of purgatory, and pour out diligent prayers for them to the Lord. For although the almighty and merciful Father, according to his justice, delays them from the kingdom, nevertheless he loves them with inestimable charity. Therefore whatever good you now do for them by praying, you offer as a pleasing sacrifice to almighty God. And when you come there, you will receive multiplied whatever you have done here in charity for them. For Scripture says: “It is a holy and wholesome thing to pray for the dead, that they may be freed from sins.”

When passing through a cemetery or cloister, pray for the dead.

When passing through a cemetery, cloister, or any other place of burial of the dead, do not forget your brothers and all the faithful departed; but, moved by charity, have compassion on them, and strive to help them before the Lord in this or a similar way.

Prayer.

You faithful souls, rest in holy peace. May he who redeemed you by his precious blood deign to free you from pains and lead you to eternal joys, where you may rejoice and exult forever, blessed ones.

Another.

May God the Father, who created you, bless you. May Jesus Christ, who redeemed you by his most precious blood, bless you. May the Holy Spirit, who by his goodness and gift preserved you from eternal damnation, bless you. Amen.

Read the following prayer often.

I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, Son of the living God, by the pain of your wounds, by the shedding of your most holy blood, and by the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on the souls of all the faithful departed who exist in the pains of purgatory, and give them a dwelling-place of eternal light with all your saints. Amen.

After vespers or the vigils of the dead, return to your cell with the customary prayers and bows. There, on bended knees, give thanks to your most merciful preserver, because he has not only graciously snatched you from the vanities of the world, but has also guarded you in the order from many evils and dangers. Then call to mind how many bodily and spiritual goods the kindly Father has bestowed on you, though you deserve nothing, and how, as the greatest reward, he has promised you himself if you faithfully persevere in his love. Be grateful, and always watchful in prayer, so that you may burn sweetly in the love of God.

At the meal.

When the signal for supper has been given, prepare yourself humbly to go to it, and observe what we marked above concerning dinner. After supper you may return to your cell and devote yourself to prayer or meditation until the signal is rung for the conference.

At the conference.

After supper, when you have heard the signal for the spiritual conference, take care to go without delay and with gravity, and to hear the last reading of the day with fervor of spirit. For the word of holy exhortation that has been heard last will cling more tenaciously to the mind throughout the whole night. But if it is a fast day, the conference is customarily observed in the refectory while drinking. Therefore be attentive to sacred reading in every place, because where the word of holy exhortation is gladly received with attention, it cannot happen that the mind is not often lifted up.

At compline.

When you come to compline, pray to the Lord that he may always make you despise all worldly and carnal things, and grant you to remain continually in his most holy love, so that, when the course of this present life has been completed, you may deserve to enter the temple of God not made by hands, and rejoice forever in the Lord with all the saints. At the end of compline, when you hear the signal of the angelic salutation being rung, humbly greet the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, that by her merits she may guard you through the night and continually intercede with her Son for your salvation.

After compline.

When compline is finished, return at once to your cell, and after a few prayers take care to prepare yourself most diligently for the following recollection of mind.

On recollection after compline. Consideration nine.

Since we cannot remain altogether unmoved in one holy state of mind, it is necessary for us often to renew our holy purpose, so that as often as during the day, by wandering through the byways of sins, we withdraw from the one principle of our soul, the most high God, so often we may return to him through contrition and compunction, with amendment firmly purposed. For this reason our holy fathers established for us that we should devote ourselves to recollection after compline and examine ourselves concerning the negligences committed during the day, so that the purpose of holiness, which we know to be quite weak and infirm, we may renew toward fervor of spirit by the continual exercise of recollection. Therefore our devout monk, wishing to recollect himself fruitfully and with useful continuance, ought principally to examine himself in order on five points.

First in recollection.

The demanding of an account.

The second is the demanding of an account, by which the monk is ordered to bring back before the eyes of the mind, for correction, whatever he remembers himself to have committed during the day by failing negligently or badly or less well. Let him turn himself to the Lord, lie before his bed with hands joined, and say in this or a similar manner: I give thanks to you, almighty and merciful God, for all your benefits, which to me, an unworthy sinner deserving absolutely nothing, from my youth [unclear] of good things.

you deigned to grant; for I, who have deserved nothing good, have received many and innumerable gifts of your goodness. Would that I could give thanks worthily to you, the highest and unchangeable good. Would that in your holy service I could praise you with a pure heart and a clean conscience. But alas, through weakness, concupiscence, and evil habit prevailing over me, I, who ought to have clung to your most holy love with a pure heart and conscience, have offended you again and again by many negligences and faults; and as often as, according to the inward inspirations of your goodness, I have tried to rise to fervor of spirit, alas, so often I grieve that I have fallen again.

Good Jesus, into how many faults, how many negligences, how many guiltinesses have I fallen today alone; how many vain, how many useless, how many harmful thoughts have I admitted in so few hours; how many useless and harmful words have I spoken; how many negligences and offenses have I committed in my actions this day.

Woe to me, miserable man, who could not persevere even one very short day in your most holy service without impurity of heart and negligence; who today have committed so many faults and various imperfections. I confess to your goodness, O most gentle God, all my sins into which I have fallen from my earliest age. Before your feet, O sweetest Jesus, I lay all the negligences that I have committed today. I ask pardon, which I am not worthy to receive; I beg for grace, which I confess that I have so often received in vain. O most loving mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, do not despise me, a miserable sinner, whom you willed to purchase with your own blood. I confess to you all the negligences into which I have in any way fallen today, and the faults that I have committed.

Here let the monk, prostrate in mind before the Lord, recall to memory the more important negligences, and, humbly asking pardon, lament his imperfection. But let him especially consider whether he has offended anyone by word or deed; whether he has said anything against a brother; whether he has committed anything against charity and reverence; or whether he has knowingly saddened anyone wrongly. And generally, in whatever he knows that he has sinned against God, against himself, against his prelate, against his neighbor, or against the rule or the statutes of the fathers, let him be eager to recall it for the examination of this chapter; and concerning secret matters in tomorrow’s confession, and concerning public and regular transgressions in the first chapter, let him faithfully and from his heart resolve to clear himself by accusing himself. Let him grieve over what has been committed; let him make satisfaction for what he has repented of; let him beware of what may be committed.

Then let him consider the grave danger of offending God, whether the sin be venial or mortal. For John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, says in his treatise On the Spiritual Life: Sin, even venial sin, is so much against God that, by his justice, he could condemn a man for it to eternal punishment. But that he does not impute it to man unto damnation proceeds not from justice but from his infinite goodness. And Saint Anselm warns us that a man ought not knowingly to commit the least sin against the will of God for the whole world. For the most blessed bishop Augustine says: No sin is so venial that it will not become mortal while it is pleasing. You will say: This opinion cannot be true, because if a sin is venial, it can never become mortal; but if it becomes mortal, it was not venial. But listen and understand. I grant that venial sin, in its own consideration, cannot become mortal; but one and the same sin, which can stand together with charity, becomes only venial in one person from mere negligence and weakness, while in another, from contempt and aversion from God in the same sin, it is without doubt mortal, if it is pleasing even insofar as it is sin and against God. Therefore blessed is he who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. Whoever neglects the smallest sins that he could amend falls little by little into graver ones.

But how much sin displeases almighty God, the punishment that follows makes plain. For in sacred books and in the deeds of times past we read that sinners have so often been severely punished against the Lord that we rightly fear the tinder of sin. How much even the briefest thought of a spirit turned away displeases him is declared to us by the fall of the first angel. For as soon as he showed himself disordered by rising up against the Lord, he was cast out.

He was in hell.

How greatly idle and useless words are against God, a sufficiently clear story in the Lives of the Holy Fathers warns us, concerning the infernal swine that appeared among brothers who were speaking useless things.

How greatly evil and pernicious words offend almighty God became plain in the five-year-old boy and blasphemer, whom the devil, snatching him from his father’s lap, carried alive to hell, as is believed.

How much [unclear] deeds and negligences concerning duty displease [God] is plain in the sons of Eli, who were negligent and took too little care over the rite of sacrifice.

How much even good works, customary ones, done [with obedience set aside?], displease God, Saint [Astion?] taught us by his own deed: although not against a [superior’s?] command, he did not carry the customary waters with impunity. And we read of many other similar cases.

But when our devout cenobite, in his recollections, finds himself burdened with things committed, or with any other negligences or sins, however grave, let him assume such contrition as is possible for him over what he has committed, a firm purpose of amendment to beware in the future, and penance for what has been committed. Therefore let him take to himself [unclear], and let him say with compunction: Truth I. Lord my God, I confess [unclear] to your most holy goodness that in this or that way I have sinned against your will. For this I grieve deeply; and because I have offended you, who are wholly good, I humbly do penance.

Truth II. Lord my God, who know all things, you know that, by your generosity, I have a good intention, and I intend, with your help, to amend myself in the future as far as I can. He should beware of sins by prayers, calling upon God for help; by inflicting penitential pains on the body; by flight, avoiding the occasion of sin. Therefore, for the third truth, let him say: Truth III. Lord my God, I have a good will to make satisfaction for my sins according to your command and that of holy mother Church, [unclear], wholly and without pretense.

Whoever has uttered these three truths to the Lord from sincerity of heart, without falsity in mouth or mind, however much he has sinned before, is now secure, if he dies in such a state even without confession in the absence of a priest; yet in such a way that in purgatory he makes satisfaction for what he has not completed by doing penance. But whoever, because of the pleasure of sinning in which he actually delights, or because of a wicked intention by which he scorns to avoid sins and their occasions, cannot truly say these same truths from a pure mind, is in a state of damnation; not even the pope can absolve him.

II. The Declaration of Future Caution

The second thing which he prescribes as to be observed by the cenobite in his recollection is called the declaration of future caution. Let him weigh what have been the occasions of his past transgression, and he will more easily guard himself from future danger. For the pit of sin is never better stopped up than if the occasion of sinning is avoided. And Saint Bernard says: To the approaching night, indeed, an announcement must be made, by distributing one’s exercises according to the rule of the common institution. In these things he duly pays every debt, if the spirit is subjected to God and the flesh to the spirit, and if anything has been omitted through negligence or imperfection, it does not remain unrecompensed in manner, time, and place.

III. Request for Suffrages

The third thing in the recollection of a good cenobite is the devout request for suffrages; for he, understanding his own weakness very well, asks help from those stronger than himself. Therefore, when he has completed his recognition [of himself?], he turns to the holy and undivided Trinity to seek mercy; then he calls upon the most blessed Mother of God; afterward he implores the prayers and aids of all the saints. And here he remembers not only himself, but pours out prayers for the whole order and for the Church.

IV. Blessing for Going to Rest

The fourth thing in the recollection is the cenobite’s blessing for going to rest, by which he fortifies himself with prayers and commits himself to the divine goodness to be guarded through the night. Therefore At the sound of the signal for sleeping, or at the appointed time, going to the place of rest, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross, and say with devotion: The peace of our Lord Jesus Christ; the merit and integrity of blessed Mary ever virgin; the sign of the holy cross; the power of the whole Passion; the blessing, protection, and merits of all the holy angels and elect of God be between me and all my enemies, visible and invisible, here and forever. Amen.

Blessing of rest

I commend myself this night and at every time.

Prayer

In your wounds, most loving Lord Jesus; and I pray you, by the merit of your most holy Passion, have mercy on me and guard me from all the snares and illusions of the enemy, so that, with a pure mind and a clean body, I may be able to perform, with the dispositions granted me, this hour that is about to be kept, and to praise you with fervor of spirit.

Discretion for obtaining rest

The fifth and last thing to be remembered in recollection is discretion in obtaining rest: just as the cenobite should never wholly omit this evening recollection, so too he should not wish to prolong it too indiscreetly to the destruction of his own head. Therefore, when all things have been completed with discretion, let the fervent desire for God, with tears if he can, raise up the mind; let it not pour it out too deeply. But when he goes up to his bed, let him carry with him in memory something of the Lord’s Passion, or of the love of Jesus, or certainly of the glory of the heavenly kingdom, in which, as he sleeps, he may rest sweetly.

For Bernard says: When you are about to go to sleep, carry something with you in memory or in thought, in which you may quietly fall asleep; which may sometimes even help you to dream; which may also receive you when you wake, and restore you to the state of yesterday’s intention. Thus the night will shine for you like the day, and your night will be light in your delights, so that you may quietly fall asleep, rest in peace, and wake easily; and when you rise you will be ready to return to that from which you had not wholly departed. Nevertheless, discretion must be applied in all these things, lest either excessive meditation, hindering sleep, destroy the brain, or sleep, taken immoderately, wholly interrupt meditation. Rather, a monk must sleep and meditate moderately, so that at the appointed time he may be disposed to rise for the divine office, with a cheerful and well-ordered mind. Affection inflamed too much by meditation destroys the brain and the senses, and takes sleep from weak eyes. Thus, then, let meditation in bed be brief, where great strength is not present in the head either by grace or by nature.

On the labor of the hands. Colide. E.

Since our most holy father Benedict, in the Rule, commending monks who live by the labor of their hands, declares them true and blessed, it has seemed fitting to us to say something after the end of the day about this most holy exercise. Indeed, we read that this work is commended by the holy fathers in many ways; and we know that in it they advanced before God and men in no small measure. For the holy Apostle says: He who does not work, let him not eat. What Augustine, more learned among the most learned, thought about this manual exercise, he shows most clearly in the book On the Work of Monks. We also read that those ancient and most holy fathers who dwelt in solitude labored fervently at the work of their hands, so that they might not incur the danger of idleness, and, living by their own labors, after the example of the most blessed teacher of the Gentiles, might burden no one. Would that we too, brothers, might deign to take up this holy exercise of laboring with the same intention and good will as they did, so that after the end of our labor we may deserve to rest with them without end in the heavenly homeland.

Four things are to be observed by a monk in labor

A monk called to labor should strive to show himself such in all things that he does not lose the merit of bodily labor through dissolution of mind. For we see many among monks go out to labor wrongly, whom we see seeking nothing other than the comforts of the flesh. Of these, some, so that during the time of fasting they may have an occasion for eating regularly, undertake useless and less necessary labors. Labo—

[unclear] so that he may eat; whether he benefits or harms the monastery he does not care. Others, so that they may be able to run about here and there, as though by occasion, without the bridle of discipline, have taken pains to arrange various labors. Others, so that they may freely indulge in vain conversations and frivolities, procure labors useless to the monastery. Others, so that they may be able, as if by opportunity and without suspicion, to see and speak with people, secular men known to them and friends after the flesh, not after God, love external labors. Others, because through instability of mind they are unable to be at rest in the monastery, always seem to pant after labors. But the intention of all who labor in this way is not sincere, and therefore they do not attain the best reward of labor.

But you, brother, when you are called to labor, take care to submit your intention to the rule’s discipline, so that you love nothing except the honor of God, the merit of obedience, and the usefulness of the monastery; intend nothing except the advancement of the soul. And when you are at work, do not imprudently extinguish the fervor of the spirit; do not omit the exercise of spiritual conversation, but take care diligently to observe everywhere the four things that follow. In outward conduct be faithful, serviceable, and kindly; inwardly, humble and devout; in speech, sparing and edifying; in manners, composed and mature. If you observe these things in labor, you will always return better to your cell.

Outwardly the monk should be faithful, kindly, and serviceable.

The first thing to be diligently observed in the labor of a cenobite is that in laboring he should always show himself faithful to his monastery; in serving and ministering, and even in carrying heavier burdens, he should anticipate the brothers out of charity; and to all, in words and deeds, he should show himself kindly and tractable. Saint Bernard, the lover of God, says: A serious and prudent soul prepares itself for every labor; nor is it dissolved in it, but through it rather gathers itself into itself, since it always has before its eyes not so much what it is doing as what it intends by doing it. For the more it aims at the end of consummation, the more truly it strives toward it, so much the more fervently and faithfully it also works with its hands, subjecting to itself the service of its whole body; in this the will creates use, use creates exercise, and exercise supplies strength.

A devout and faithful cenobite, who loves God in truth, does not spare himself in labor, but with great fervor, cheerfulness, and fidelity is accustomed to apply himself to the works of the hands imposed on him, just as if by his labor alone he were compelled to feed all those established in the monastery. For the most prudent soul has learned to expend itself wholly for God, whatever bodily necessity may have made it labor in his service. For just as spiritual things cannot long subsist in religion without the cooperation of temporal things, so I do not hesitate to call him a servant of God who for God’s sake ministers the bodily necessities to those serving God. And therefore whatever a good cenobite, by his labors and with right intention, can acquire for the monastery, let him know that he offers all of it to the Lord. Nevertheless, the monk should always understand that he must labor in such a way that he by no means omits the monastic prayers, masses, and the other services of holy mother Church.

Manual work, however, undertaken out of curiosity and personal complacency, is deprived of the merit of obedience before the eternal Judge; and, as idle and undertaken without the superior’s permission, it is held subject to the strictest accounting. But the good cenobite, who desires to please God alone, in every stealthy intrusion of an idle word, deed, or thought, should say this saying of Bernard within himself: If you were now about to die, would you do this thing which you now do, think, or say? Since you would not do now, if you were about to die, what you are now doing, you are most foolish, for, being about to die in a short time, you so boldly permit yourself acts worthy of death. But if, since it is necessary, you desire to die well, never do at any time what you would not do if death were already present. For whatever you do now, after death you will find it, whether good or bad.

Inwardly the monk should be humble and devout.

Second, the monk, beneath the covering of labor, ought inwardly to be devout and humble, since if he has lost the inner progress of fervor, it does not help that through labor he acquires outwardly. Therefore, so that in laboring the spirit may truly advance, let him often bring back to memory the degrees of good will written in the first [region?]. Let him order meditations on the Lord’s passion with the fervor of devotion, in which, according to the possibility of his labor, he may conform his labors to Christ’s labor. Let there always be in his heart humble self-denial. Let him be devout in affection with the fervor of holy union, so that the labor of the hand outwardly may advance toward the perfection and usefulness of the community, and the mind may not withdraw from the eternal sweetness of divine love. If labor wearies the monk at work, if heat burns him, if untimely thirst or hunger afflicts him, let him call to mind how many labors the Lord Jesus sustained for us, and he will bear all things lightly. Therefore, praying, let him say to the Lord: Most sweet and most loving Prayer of one who labors. Lord Jesus, king of heaven and earth, who for my redemption were born of the most pure Virgin Mary, and for thirty-three years lived among men as God and man; who had great labors in walking, teaching, and preaching; who for me willingly and patiently endured weariness, hunger, heat, and cold: for all these things I give you thanks. Receive, I beseech you, my very small labors, however useless, which I humbly offer to your most holy majesty in memory and honor of all your labors and of your most holy passion; and may they be pleasing to you in that union in which your labors were most pleasing to God the Father. Amen.

But under labor, if time permits, let our monk turn over the principal articles of the Lord’s passion: first those which were present to Christ in the passion by commemoration; then at his knees by giving thanks; third, by asking mercy in them according to [their?] common likeness.

Let him also recall to memory the conversations of the holy fathers or the passions of the martyrs, and consider how great a reward and glory they now receive in the fatherland for their labors.

In speech let the monk be sparing and edifying

[Unclear] what must be observed by the monk in labor, [unclear].

...is laid down: namely, that he should say few things, and things that edify. For Scripture says, "In much speaking sin will not be lacking." A monk should not speak without permission, if he truly desires to be good. But when permission to speak has been granted, let him say only few and useful things; and let him know that idle and jesting words are condemned by the Rule in every place. Let him establish for himself such a manner of speaking, with circumspection in every place and time, that by speaking he offend no one. Let him be more willing to listen than pleased to speak; nor let him say those things that [unclear] suggests, if he fears the reproach of fools. For thus Hugh says to the monk: Do not pour out everything that I know, like a vessel without a lid, which, as soon as it is tilted, pours out whatever it contains, and lies open to every dust and filth. Carefully beware lest you seem, directly or indirectly, to seek your own glory, or imprudently reveal to anyone, from a desire for boasting, something praiseworthy that lies hidden in you, or [unclear]. If you keep silent about yourself and conceal it, you will be more pleasing; if you bring yourself forward and commend yourself, you will become worthless before all and will be mocked. Beware of idle words, because while we do not attend to such things, we slip little by little into harmful ones, from which are generated either [unclear] or dissolutions or grievous corrodings of patience. Be such in your inner way of life that, through love of spiritual meditation, silence delights you much more than talkativeness.

In his conduct let the cenobite be composed and mature.

Fourth, a monk ought, whether at work or outside it, in every place, to compose his [unclear] manners [unclear], and in all things, both in deeds and in words, to show himself mature before men. Thus in [unclear].

...has this as its own proper feature of progress: that it makes the mind of the one striving very circumspect in all things. But he who does not have a firm effort to make progress toward the better certainly cannot truly be called composed, although to men he may seem to be mature. For feigned maturity quickly dissolves into open dissolution of mind, where it does not have the fear of God as the root of discipline. Therefore, so that our cenobite may always be composed within and without, let him strive to be truly rooted in the fear of the Lord. For he who fears God neglects nothing. And the love of God is not idle.

What the conduct of a monk toward other people ought to be.

Since, indeed, we have begun to speak of the maturity and composure that a monk must preserve before men, it seems useful to us now to say briefly how he ought to present himself to each person. For he is instructed to present himself in one way to his superior, and in another way he is commanded to show himself to his confreres and to secular persons. To the rector, as standing in the place of Christ, he ought to show reverence; to his confrere, charity; to those who trouble him, gentleness; to secular persons, modest piety. And so let the monk render to each one what is his, and he will be truly composed before God and men. What he owes to God, and what to himself, has been sufficiently said above; now let us pursue what has been set before us.

Let his conduct be reverential toward the prelate, as standing in the place of Christ.

First, the conduct of a monk ought to be reverential toward the prelate, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who spurns you spurns me.” For the monk who withholds due obedience and reverence from his abbot does injury to almighty God. For, as our most holy father says in the Rule, the abbot is proved to hold the place of Christ in the monastery. Whoever, therefore, despises the vicar of any king has beyond doubt despised the king himself. But tell me, good brother, why do you withhold such reverence from your prelate, whom you hear called the vicar of Christ? Perhaps you judge him wicked and utterly unworthy of such an office, and for that reason you think it lawful for you to despise him. Not so, brother, not so; but consider whose place this is, in which the vicar of Christ sits, and know that you must honor the one who sends, not the one sent. If you wish to be a disciple of Christ, always consider why you came, and you will never deny reverence even to an unworthy prelate. For why did you come? Certainly so that, according to the rule of the Gospel, you might deny yourself for God’s sake; that under another’s command you might serve as a soldier for Christ; that with patience you might await the eternal reward promised to you. Therefore, brother, do not, do not lose the crown of eternal happiness prepared for you in heaven because of the displeasure caused by one man, a crown which you ought not exchange for the whole world. Remember that you have nothing except from God, to whom you owe all that you are and all that you know, so that you may fulfill his will and live according to his ordinance. But since you cannot trust yourself to be able to understand the will of God, you ought humbly to obey your rector, as his sacred vicar to whom you have subjected yourself; nor ought you to scrutinize either his life or his command, since it is not lawful for you to judge your shepherd. Indeed, in your profession you swore that you must not carry out your own will, but that you wished to obey the abbot in all things according to the Rule. The abbot, therefore, is the lord of your will, not by his own presumption, but by the ordinance of God, whose servant and vicar he is. But the handling of another’s property against the owner’s will is theft; and you know that thieves will have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God. And so a monk, professed according to the Rule to God and to his abbot, henceforth does not have his own [unclear] of his will; if afterward he has usurped his own will for himself, he commits theft and sacrilege. Nor will permission obtained save the presumptuous man, if it has been obtained by prayers and insults. Your abbot, O brother, is the vicar of God, to whom you ought to render the obedience you promised, not as to a good man, but as to holy God.

[unclear]: to show him humble reverence in the place of God. Whatever is bestowed by subjects upon a rector will without doubt be referred to God, whose vicar he is. Since, therefore, you have subjected yourself to your prelate for God alone and for no other cause, you should strive at all times to show yourself such toward him that he may freely be able to command you to do or leave undone whatever seems expedient to him, and need not fear any insolence or disturbances of your mind at all. For if your abbot is compelled to fear you, his monk, the order of equity is violated; and where the disciple strives to be above the master, sin is committed against the Gospel. Therefore beware lest you withhold reverence and honor from prelates; beware lest you offend them by saddening them, but take care to meet them, whatever sort of men they may be, with reverence, and in all things to obey their commands according to the Gospel and the Rule. Believe me, brother, because the fault committed by a subject against a prelate is punished very severely, either in the present life or in the life to come. For it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones. Whatever your prelate has commanded you, you ought to receive with such confidence that you believe God inspired it in him.

Let the monk’s manner of life toward the brethren be charitable.

Second, the monk’s manner of life toward his confrères is commanded to have charity; through this alone peace and concord are maintained in the monastery. Let our faithful cenobite always think upon and turn over in his heart the common joy of souls in eternal happiness, and let him continually direct the eye of his mind toward the equal condition of souls, so that his thought may not withdraw from love of their future fellowship. If a brother has offended you in any way by word or deed, if he has been troublesome or contrary to you in anything, do not weigh the disordered movement of sensuality from this; do not consider his present weakness, but lift the eyes of your mind to the nobility of his soul, and consider what fellowship of eternal happiness it will have with you. To this end you ought to bring back to memory the chapter of the Rule on the good zeal of monks, so that you may more easily rouse yourself to brotherly charity. Before all things, beware lest you admit displeasure against your brother, for he who is often accustomed to be angry with his neighbor clearly proves that he does not love God. For whoever loves God with his whole heart does not admit displeasure against his faithful brother. Indeed, a monk ought to be established in such great elevation of mind that, whatever a brother has committed against him, by considering the nature of that soul he cannot be moved.

Let the monk’s manner of life toward those who do injury be meek.

Third, the monk’s manner of life toward those who do injury ought to be meek, for then at last it is done well if regard is always had for the common future happiness and fellowship. To attain this meekness of spirit, let the cenobite learn to bring more frequently to mind the lives of the holy fathers, and faithfully to consider with how much joy they received injuries. Let him strive first of all, as far as possible, to imitate our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who not only endured the injuries and insults of the impious with a most meek heart, but also prayed to the Father for his persecutors, that they should not perish. Imitating this example of the Savior, the holy fathers were accustomed patiently and meekly to receive injuries for the love of God, and, what is more, to love those very injurers. To this end let the cenobite recall to mind the degrees of meekness, which are contained briefly in these verses: Be apt, strengthen, as a meek man bear contrary things. Preserve, restrain, rest wholly with yourself. Correct prudently, be merciful, give wisely. Pray by setting yourself down, by desiring martyrdom. For if humility has possessed the mind of the cenobite, it makes him love injuries. The degrees of humility are contained in these verses.

The twelve degrees of humility.

The first of these degrees fears the Almighty. The second sets reins upon the enticements of the flesh. The third submits itself reverently to the abbot.

Pressed by insults, the fourth patiently obeys. The fifth reports the depths of his heart to the abbot. The sixth, by his own judgment, is sure that he is [useless?] and unworthy. Then the seventh believes himself to be lower than all. The eighth does nothing that the rule of the cell does not permit. The ninth does not speak until another asks him. The tenth proscribes laughter and condemns guffawing. The eleventh speaks a few words of reason. The twelfth always looks at the ground with head bent.

On the same, otherwise.

[Fear] God, and do not do your own will; let another govern you. Bear [hard things?]; conceal nothing in your heart, but also seek the lowest things. Be refuse; do not wander alone; shut your tongue. Let laughter be sparing, speech grave, gestures humble.

Note: peripsema ought to be read and written, not peripsima, as the ignorant read in the Epistle to the [Corinthians?]; and it means filings and the cleansing of all things.

Thus the monk’s conduct toward secular persons is modest.

Fourth, the monk’s conduct toward secular persons ought to be modest, so that neither his familiarity with them be excessive nor his withdrawal indiscreet. Hence Hugh says: “Toward all persons, as far as lies in you, beware of everything that can fail to be a good example for them,” just as it befits the faithful servant of God to promote in all things the honor of his Lord, and to guard against his dishonor. Do not be familiar with any woman, even a holy one. For if they are discreet, you will please them more by this; but if they are importunate, they are to be avoided all the more. Be [unclear]. Be obliging to the weak, humble in [services?]; be very truthful in words; let your words be as an oath, and edifying to others. Love poverty. Be chaste in all things, and everywhere reverent.

But in founding all virtues and good morals, set before yourself that most glorious and most perfect example of all brightness: the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent from heaven for this, that he might go before us in the way of virtues and teach us by his example to follow himself. Therefore, the more the monk takes care to conform himself to him by imitation in the way of virtues, so much the more like and nearer to him he will without doubt be in the glory of eternal felicity. Whatever you do, always look to him, and consider how he bore himself in all things according to the Gospel and according to your own estimation. For you know this very well: he bore himself most excellently in all things. Say therefore to yourself: If my Lord Jesus were present, what do you think he would do in this matter? Or what would he now say? Certainly he would both act and speak most excellently; I ought, according to my powers, to imitate him in all things.

General conclusion of all spiritual exercises.

Wishing at length to put some end to this work, we say that the completion of all spiritual exercises consists in two things. First, in knowledge and perception of one’s own imperfection, so that the monk may always be conscious of his weakness and remain rooted in humility. Second, in the desire and effort to come to a higher manner of life, so that he may always desire to advance in spirit to better things and may in no way withdraw from this effort. Every cenobite ought to stretch out his mind at every moment toward this effort of advancement; if he ever neglects it, he incurs transgression of his vow and very grave danger to his soul. But let the monk beware lest consideration of his own weakness lead him away from the effort of advancing; let him beware lest that effort itself despise consideration of imperfection. Rather, let these two cohere with each other mutually in such a way that neither ever withdraws from the other. But if excessive consideration of his own imperfection attempts to lead the mind into despair, let him recall to memory what the holy abbot Bernard said: “Let us breathe again, brothers, because although we are nothing in our own hearts, perhaps something can lie hidden in us in the heart of God.” These two considerations, of our weakness and of divine estimation, excite great devotion in us, as the psalmist said: “I am poor and sorrowful”; behold the first. “Your salvation, O God, has upheld me”; behold the second.

Furthermore, it is necessary for one who wishes to occupy himself usefully in these spiritual exercises to have a joyful and free heart, and one estranged from every anxiety or care of the world. For the Holy Spirit is the spirit of freedom and joy; he loves a heart free and joyful in God, and, so to speak, applauds what is like himself. For just as a bird bound on the ground cannot lift itself up to heaven by flying, so a mind occupied with perishable things cannot raise itself to heavenly things. Nor ought one to cast down the spirit by excessive repetition of these things; otherwise the brain too is confused, and one labors in vain by dry habit. Therefore let the cenobite learn, fervent in spirit, always to persist in these things with moderation, and continually to refer the cause of every exercise, through intention, to God, who is the beginning and end of all goodness. Let him faithfully direct his effort to fear and love of him, and fix his mind in deep humility, since he who is rooted in love is not easily abandoned by God.

Here is the end of the Spiritual Exercise of Cloistered Persons, by Peter of Friedberg in the noble city of [Hagenau?], on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the year of salvation 1498.

Here begins the compendium of spiritual exercise. Johannes Trithemius.

This form of spiritual exercise, issued by us for the edification of cloistered persons, might appear very brief to all devout persons who have leisure; yet we fear that to those sufficiently occupied in household affairs it may seem rather lengthy. For when thought is stretched by continual solicitude in arranging necessary matters [unclear], the mind is easily wearied in spiritual exercises, even the very briefest. Therefore, lest our monks who are either devoted to external things or less devout in spiritual conversation should be able, on the occasion of prolixity, to flee loosely to an argument of excuse, we have been ordered to abbreviate the same instruction, so that both the more fervent in their devotion may retain the greater one, and the lukewarm may not omit the lesser.

There follows the practice of spiritual exercise.

At all and each of the hours generally, let the devout cenobite strive to direct his effort to this end: that with all his strength he may desire to magnify God in his heart as the root of His benefits. Let there be in him so very fervent an ardor of devotion, so much compunction, so great an inundation of tears coming on, that whoever sees him chanting the psalms may be moved by his example to magnify the Lord. Secondly, let him remember that he can be stirred up to the charity of the first [unclear]; for love is directed toward God in vain if the neighbor is hated. Therefore, when all the thorns of displeasure have been expelled, let the most devout cenobite, turned toward God, pray.

O almighty, everlasting God, who, instructing us for the exercise of Your love by the manifold creation of things, have commanded us to love You above all things with all our strength and our neighbor as ourselves for Your sake: graciously grant me the grace of Your most holy love and of love of neighbor, so that, all motions of displeasure, aversion, and anger being restrained, I may love You always with a pure heart above all things, and may in no way withdraw from sincere love of neighbor; so that, just as a member joined to a member suffers with one that is injured, so may my mind, sincerely loving its neighbor, deserve to be a member of our true head, Jesus Christ. Who lives and reigns with You.

Another Prayer.

I beseech You, holy Father, almighty eternal God, by the virtue of the most holy passion of Your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: enlighten the eyes of my heart, that, pierced by the spirit, I may see how often I have offended in Your commandments; and, cleansed by Your mercy from every filth of sin, may I never offend You hereafter.

After Matins.

When Matins has ended, while still remaining in the church, or also when placed in your cell, take up for yourself the disposition of true resignation, praying thus.

Prayer.

Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who at the morning hour, set in the greatest anguish of Your most holy heart, after a threefold prayer fully resigned Yourself into the will of God the Father: grant me, by the virtue of that charity of Yours, perfectly to despise my own will in all things for love of You, and truly to resign myself at all times into the disposition of Your will and of those whom You have placed over me. Who live and reign.

After Prime.

After Prime, when, leaving the choir, you enter the chapter place, in memory of your most innocent Savior accused before Pilate, you will form your disposition toward humble confession, praying thus to the Lord.

Prayer.

[unclear]

You were given vinegar to drink and were mocked in many ways: I ask You, by the pain of Your wounds, grant me pardon for all my sins, the grace of holy compunction, a fountain of tears, the deep virtue of humility, and continual remembrance of Your most bitter passion, so that all that I am and am able to do may always serve You, and my mind may continually burn in Your love.

After None.

After None, be mindful of sweetest Jesus dying on the cross, and, hastening in spirit to His knees, to whom with tears you can give thanks with devout [unclear], you will pray thus.

I pray You, sweetest [unclear]: Lord Jesus Christ, king of heaven and earth, have mercy on me, for whom you died on the cross; and I humbly give thanks to you for your holy passion and most innocent death. O most loving Savior, what shall I render to you for all the things that you have rendered to me? Behold, I offer myself to you; I continually desire to dwell in your most holy wounds. I ask you, by the virtue of your most innocent death, have mercy on me as you know how; fasten my flesh with your fear, and restrain in me all disordered motions, so that, inflamed by the fervor of your most holy love, I may love you with a pure heart, confess you praiseworthy with my mouth, and follow you in deed, according to my strength, in humble conduct. I beseech you, most merciful Lord Jesus, by that anguish of your most holy heart which you endured on the cross, when your most holy soul departed from your body: have mercy on my soul at its departure.

The first hour after dinner.

The first hour after dinner. Unless you are occupied with higher exercises, for first obtaining knowledge of frailty, pray for the day in this or a similar manner.

Prayer

Almighty God, who out of your great goodness created me in the first parent from the mud of the earth, so that, mindful of my humble condition, I might glorify you, my creator, in true humility: grant me, I beseech you, truly to know my frailty in all things, so that, while I consider that I am both vile and almost nothing by my own merit, I may first deserve to please you by your gift. Through Christ.

The Second Hour.

At the second hour after midday let our cenobite bring back to memory the gravity of sins, both his own and those by which, especially while living in holy religion, he has sinned against the rule; and, turned toward the Lord, let him pray thus.

Prayer

Almighty everlasting God, who deigned, from your mercy alone, to make us wretched ones, dead in sins, alive by the incarnation and death of your only-begotten Son, our Jesus Christ: grant me, by the virtue of his most innocent passion, indulgence for all my sins and my own, so that henceforth I may deserve to serve you with a pure conscience. Through the same our Lord.

The Third Hour.

At the third hour after dinner let our faithful cenobite remember his vows and what he promised the Lord, and especially the renunciation of all property, namely in things, [unclear], and will; and, compunct in fervor of spirit, he shall pray thus to the Lord.

Prayer

Almighty and merciful God, who by kindly favor sanctify and receive the vows of your servants, offered to you from faithful devotion: grant me to render all that has been promised to you, and the virtue of humility, chastity, obedience, and poverty, with such purity of mind that I may deserve, with your mercy, to obtain your kingdom promised to the poor in spirit. Through our Lord.

After vespers:

After vespers let our good cenobite think that all visible things are vain; and, raised in mind to the love of invisible goods and to the Lord, let him cry out with as much devotion as he can.

Prayer.

Almighty everlasting God, who wished to lead us through the visible things which you created to knowledge and love of invisible things: grant me so to know the vanity of present things that I may deserve to think on the eternity of future things with a pure and [unclear] mind.

Another.

God, protector of those who hope in you, without whom nothing is strong, nothing holy: multiply your mercy upon us, so that, with you as ruler, with you as guide, we may so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose eternal goods.

Another prayer.

God, who have prepared invisible good things for those who love you: pour into our hearts the affection of your love, so that, loving you in all things and above all things, we may obtain your promises, which surpass every desire. Through the Lord.

After supper and collation:

After supper or collation let the most faithful cenobite put on desire for good zeal, and especially for souls, with what fervor of charity he can; and, praying to the Lord, let him say.

Prayer.

Lord God, greatest lover of faithful souls, who wished your Son to die on the gibbet of the cross for the salvation of men: grant me, by the example of the same your Son, always to make progress in good zeal, and to fear no labors, no adversities, for the salvation of souls, so that, strengthened by the fire of your love, I may dare to resist in due season those who contradict you; and manfully set myself as a wall for your house. Through the same our Lord.

After Compline

After Compline, having gathered his powers, the devout cenobite should enter alone into the secret place of his heart; let him leave all cares and anxieties outside, bare of them, so that, free and released from all things, he may deserve to speak with the Lord Jesus through the desire of compunction, and sweetly to be united through the burning of love. Thus, having recalled the faults of the day in summary to the memory for examination, let him pray to the Lord as follows.

Prayer.

O most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, who for our redemption willed to undergo a most shameful death: grant me, I beseech you, through the pain of your wounds and through the shedding of your most holy blood, and through the power of your most innocent death, pardon for all my sins, so that with conscience cleansed I may hereafter cling to you continually through the desire of love; may make daily progress in holy religion; and may humbly submit myself in all things to your most holy will.

To the Son.

My body and my soul I commend to you, Lord Jesus Christ, this night and at every time, in the power and union of that love by which, hanging on the cross, you commended your beloved mother, the Virgin Mary, to the disciple. In that love, I beseech you, guard me from all the snares of the ancient serpent; suppress the unlawful motions of the flesh; drive far away foul and evil dreams; and repel the phantasms of the nights, so that I may sleep secure in your peace, and at the hours appointed for me may rise gladly to your praises. Amen.

To the Father.

Lord, holy Father, almighty, eternal God, who kindly received us into your grace in the passion of your only-begotten Son: receive, I beseech you, mercifully, all the good things, bestowed by you, that I have done on this day, in words, deeds, and thoughts, in the power and union of that charity and love by which you received the same your Son hanging and dying on the cross for us. And to you, holy Father, in the faith and union of that charity I commend myself this night and at every time, by which your Son, our Lord, when now about to die, commended his spirit to you on the cross.

To Saint Mary.
